rationale: src/auth/auth.service.ts is cohesive: AuthService covers login, social login, registration, email confirmation, password reset, profile update, token refresh and logout. It also has one shared helper, the private getTokensData, which builds access and refresh tokens. That helper is the right pattern, but the file does not follow it for two other security rules. (1) The rule for making a session hash, crypto.createHash('sha256').update(randomStringGenerator()).digest('hex'), is written out separately in validateLogin, validateSocialLogin and refreshToken. (2) The email-confirmation token is signed with auth.confirmEmailSecret and auth.confirmEmailExpires, and that code is copied in register and update. It is verified with the same secret in two near-identical blocks, in confirmEmail and confirmNewEmail. The session-plus-token issuing sequence (sessionService.create then getTokensData) is also repeated in validateLogin and validateSocialLogin, and the bcrypt.compare password check appears in both validateLogin and update. If one copy is changed and another is missed, the behaviour drifts apart. This meets the rubric's failure condition: a rule or invariant is repeated instead of living in one place.
violation_messages: The session-hash rule (sha256 of randomStringGenerator()) is copied in validateLogin, validateSocialLogin and refreshToken. It should be one private helper, like getTokensData. | Confirmation-token signing (auth.confirmEmailSecret / auth.confirmEmailExpires) is copied in register and update. Verification with the same secret and 'invalidHash' error is copied in confirmEmail and confirmNewEmail. The token rule is not kept in one place. | validateLogin and validateSocialLogin repeat the same session-creation and token-issuing sequence instead of sharing one helper.

rationale: The unit has one file, src/auth-google/auth-google.service.ts, and it covers one concern: checking a Google ID token and turning its payload into the shared SocialInterface profile. AuthGoogleService has one public method, getProfileByToken. It uses the module's own AuthGoogleLoginDto as input and returns SocialInterface. The error format it throws (UnprocessableEntityException with status and errors) follows the usual project style. There is no unrelated logic and no bypassed module abstraction. The file reads 'google.clientId' twice. The constructor uses configService.get and getProfileByToken uses getOrThrow. This is a small inconsistency in how the same config value is read, but it is not a duplicated business rule or invariant, so it does not fail the rubric.

Both files deal with one concern: Google social login at the presentation layer. AuthGoogleModule declares AuthGoogleController and provides AuthGoogleService. The controller does no work of its own. It hands token-to-profile resolution to AuthGoogleService.getProfileByToken and the shared social-login rules to AuthService.validateSocialLogin. No rule or invariant is repeated in either file, and neither file goes around the module's abstractions. The module imports AuthModule, which is how AuthService gets injected, so the controller's dependency on it is properly declared.

Both files cover one concern: the shapes of decoded JWT payloads that the auth strategies use. jwt-payload.type.ts defines the access-token payload (JwtPayloadType). jwt-refresh-payload.type.ts defines the refresh-token payload (JwtRefreshPayloadType). Both build their fields from the domain types instead of redefining them. They use Session['id'] and Session['hash'], and Pick<User, 'id' | 'role'>, so the field types stay defined in one place. Both types repeat the standard JWT claims `iat: number; exp: number;`. These are just two standard JWT fields, not a business rule or invariant, so the repetition is too small to count as duplication under the rubric. The files don't split into unrelated concerns, and they don't bypass any of the module's own abstractions.

This unit has a single file, src/database/seeds/document/seed.module.ts. It declares one NestJS module, SeedModule, and that module has one job: setting up the document (Mongoose) seeding run. It imports UserSeedModule, loads the global config (databaseConfig and appConfig) and connects to Mongoose through the shared MongooseConfigService. It doesn't copy the connection setup inline, and it doesn't restate any rule or invariant that already lives elsewhere. It also stays within the module's own abstractions, because it reuses the existing config factories and the config service. I found no split into unrelated concerns, no duplicated rule and no bypass.

The unit is a single file, user-seed.module.ts. It declares one NestJS module, UserSeedModule. That module does one job: it registers the Mongoose User schema with MongooseModule.forFeature, then provides and exports UserSeedService. This is ordinary wiring for a NestJS seed module. The file holds no business rules or invariants that could be duplicated. It uses the existing UserSchemaClass and UserSchema exports rather than redefining the schema, so it doesn't bypass any abstraction. Whether a seed module should reach into users/infrastructure is an import-direction question, which is out of scope here.

The unit is a single file, src/files/infrastructure/persistence/file.repository.ts. It declares one abstract class, FileRepository, which acts as the persistence port for the File aggregate. It has three methods: create, findById and findByIds. All three are written in terms of the domain FileType and the shared NullableType utility. The file covers one concern (persisting and fetching files) and contains no logic, so no rule or invariant is repeated here. It also doesn't go around any abstraction: the document and relational adapters implement it, and the services and uploaders receive it through constructor injection, which is how the abstraction is meant to be used. Import direction is out of scope.

This unit has only one file, file.entity.ts. That file declares a single TypeORM persistence entity, FileEntity, which maps to the 'file' table and has two columns: a uuid primary key (id) and path. It handles one concern, relational persistence mapping, and builds on the shared base class EntityRelationalHelper instead of working around it. Nothing in it repeats a rule or invariant, and it holds no logic or abstraction that belongs elsewhere. The layer classification is a little odd: the path matches the domain pattern **/*.entity.ts, but the file sits under infrastructure/persistence. Layer and import-direction questions are out of scope for this rule, though.

The unit is a single file, src/home/home.service.ts, and it handles one concern: returning application info for the home endpoint. It reads configuration through the typed ConfigService<AllConfigType> abstraction using infer: true. It does not read process.env directly, it does not repeat any rule or invariant, and it has no unrelated responsibilities. The module is cohesive and uses its abstractions consistently.

The unit is a single file, src/mailer/mailer.service.ts, and it handles one concern: sending email. It sets up a nodemailer transporter from the mail.* config keys, optionally turns a Handlebars template into HTML, and fills in a default sender. Template rendering and the default sender are both part of preparing an outgoing message, so the file does not split into unrelated concerns. Each rule lives in one place: the transport settings are read once in the constructor, and the default sender and HTML fallback are each decided once in sendMail. The service always sends through its own transporter field and never works around it. Because the unit has only one file, there is no second file where a rule could be duplicated.

The unit has one file, src/roles/domain/role.ts, and it covers one concern: the Role domain shape, with an `id` and an optional `name`. Nothing in the file splits into unrelated concerns, and no rule within the unit is defined twice. The module has no other abstractions inside it that this file could bypass. The `idType` derivation reads `databaseConfig().isDocumentDatabase` to pick String or Number. Other domain classes may repeat that pattern, but those classes are outside this unit, so the material provided can't show duplication. Two possible concerns belong to layer or dependency checks, which are out of scope here: the domain file uses framework decorators (`@ApiProperty`, `@Allow`), and it imports database config.

The unit has one file, role.entity.ts. It declares one TypeORM persistence entity, RoleEntity, for the 'role' table. It extends the shared base EntityRelationalHelper, which is the same abstraction other relational entities use. The file has one concern and no duplicated rule or invariant. It doesn't bypass any abstraction of its own module. The file is labelled as the domain layer even though it lives under infrastructure/persistence, but that's a layer-classification question and out of scope here.

The unit has a single file, a NestJS module that wires up document (Mongoose) persistence for sessions. It registers the Session schema with MongooseModule.forFeature and binds the abstract SessionRepository port to the SessionDocumentRepository implementation. It exports only that abstraction. This is one cohesive concern, and it goes through the module's own abstraction: consumers get the abstract SessionRepository token rather than the concrete class. The file repeats no rule or invariant. Import direction and layer classification are out of scope.

This unit is a single file with one class, SessionDocumentRepository, which implements the SessionRepository port on top of Mongoose. Every method deals with storing sessions (find, create, update, update by hash, and the three delete methods), so the file covers one concern. The module's own abstractions are used consistently: all conversions between documents and the domain go through SessionMapper.toDomain/toPersistence, and all queries go through the injected Model<SessionSchemaClass>. Two small points do not amount to a violation. First, the list of fields that cannot be changed (id, createdAt, updatedAt, deletedAt) appears twice: once as the delete statements in update() and once in the Omit type in updateByHash(). Both are in the same file and follow the shape of the port contract, so this is not a rule copied across files. Second, updateByHash() writes { hash: payload.hash } directly to the model instead of passing it through the mapper. That only changes the value of a field the schema and the domain share, so it does not get around the mapping layer for domain-to-document conversion. The result is still mapped back through SessionMapper.toDomain.

The unit has one file, a NestJS module that wires up relational persistence for sessions. It registers SessionEntity with TypeOrmModule.forFeature and binds the abstract SessionRepository port to the concrete SessionRelationalRepository. It exports only the abstract port, so consumers depend on the module's abstraction and not on the concrete class. The file covers a single concern, has no duplicated rules or invariants, and does not bypass any abstraction.

The unit has one file, session.entity.ts, which declares one TypeORM persistence entity, SessionEntity. It does one job: it maps the 'session' table. It extends the shared EntityRelationalHelper base class, as relational entities in this project normally do, so it uses the module's own abstraction instead of going around it. It keeps no rule or invariant that could be duplicated, because it holds only column and relation mappings. It uses UserEntity only to declare a ManyToOne relation, which is ordinary entity-to-entity mapping and does not mix in a second concern. The layer model labels this path as 'domain' because of the **/*.entity.ts pattern, even though the file sits under infrastructure/persistence. That is a layer-classification question, which is out of scope for this rule.

The unit is one file, src/users/users.service.ts. It covers one concern, user management, and consistently uses its own repository and FilesService. However, create() and update() each contain their own inline copy of the same five rules: password hashing, email uniqueness, photo existence, role-enum membership and status-enum membership. Each copy builds the same UnprocessableEntityException payload. These rules should each live in one place. The copies have already drifted apart. In create(), any existing user with the email is a conflict. In update(), the conflict check is skipped when the existing user is the same user (userObject.id !== id). update() also adds a password check that create() lacks: it compares the stored hash to the plaintext DTO password before re-hashing. This shows that the duplicated invariants are diverging, which is the failure the rubric describes.
violation_messages: Role and status enum-membership validation (RoleEnum/StatusEnum `.map(String).includes(...)` plus the 'roleNotExists'/'statusNotExists' exceptions) is written out in full in both create() and update() instead of in one shared validator. | The photo-existence rule (filesService.findById plus the 'imageNotExists' exception and null handling) is duplicated across create() and update(). | Password hashing (bcrypt.genSalt/bcrypt.hash) and the email-uniqueness check ('emailAlreadyExists') are each implemented twice, and the copies have drifted: update() excludes the same user and adds a hash-vs-plaintext comparison that create() does not have. Each rule should live in one place.

rationale: This unit is a single file that declares one abstract class, UserRepository. The class is the persistence port for the User aggregate. All of its members deal with one concern: storing and fetching User entities. It uses the domain abstraction (User, User['id'] and similar) the same way throughout. It holds no implementation logic, so no rule or invariant is repeated, and it does not route around any of the module's own abstractions. The document and relational repositories both implement it, and UsersService injects it, so it works as the module's single contract. It does use FilterUserDto and SortUserDto from the application DTOs, but that is a layer-dependency question, which is out of scope here.

The unit has one file, user.repository.ts, which declares one class, UsersDocumentRepository. That class implements the UserRepository port for MongoDB persistence, so the module covers one concern: storing and loading User aggregates through the Mongoose model. Every method converts between storage and domain shapes with the module's own UserMapper (toPersistence/toDomain) and never maps objects by hand, so the abstraction is used consistently. The id-to-_id translation and the null-guard lookups are written inline in a few methods. This is normal repository work and does not duplicate a domain invariant that belongs elsewhere. The update method rebuilds the full domain object from the stored document and the payload, then runs it back through the mapper, so the mapping rule stays in one place. I found no split concerns, no duplicated invariant and no bypass of the module's abstractions.

This module has a single file, user.entity.ts, and it covers one concern: the TypeORM mapping for the 'user' table. It declares one class, UserEntity, which extends the project's shared EntityRelationalHelper base class, so it uses the project's own persistence abstraction instead of going around it. Its relations point at the matching relational entity classes from the files, roles and statuses modules (FileEntity, RoleEntity, StatusEntity), so the abstraction stays the same throughout. The default value for the provider column comes from AuthProvidersEnum.email rather than a repeated literal, so that rule lives in one place. Nothing is split across unrelated concerns, nothing is duplicated, and no abstraction is bypassed. The file is matched to the domain layer even though it sits under infrastructure, but that is a layer-mapping question and out of scope here.

src/app.module.ts falls under the presentation layer because of the **/*.module.ts pattern. In NestJS, module files are where the app is wired together. This file is the root module: it imports feature modules, registers config loaders, sets up i18n and picks which database module to load. It has no business rules, no domain logic and no request handling. The one part that touches persistence is the `infrastructureDatabaseModule` block, which uses `isDocumentDatabase` to choose between `MongooseModule.forRootAsync` and `TypeOrmModule.forRootAsync`. That block hands the real setup to `MongooseConfigService` or `TypeOrmConfigService`, and its `dataSourceFactory` is the standard one-line `new DataSource(options).initialize()`. This is how the framework registers modules, not repository or query code, so it belongs in a module file. The rubric's Fail examples are business rules in presentation or infrastructure, or persistence or framework logic in domain. Neither applies here, so the file's responsibilities fit the role a module file plays in the presentation layer. Confidence is moderate, because a stricter reading could call the database-selection block infrastructure configuration.

The file is a NestJS @Module declaration and does only module wiring: it lists the modules it imports, its providers, its exports and its controllers. This composition and wiring role fits the presentation layer, which the layer model assigns to **/*.module.ts. The file contains no business rules, persistence logic or transport handling.

AuthService is declared application-layer. Its use-case orchestration fits that role: login, social login, registration, email confirmation, password reset, profile update and token refresh, all done by calling UsersService, SessionService and MailService. But the file also builds HTTP transport responses throughout. It throws UnprocessableEntityException, NotFoundException and UnauthorizedException from @nestjs/common, and puts explicit HTTP status codes (HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY, HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND) inside the error bodies. Mapping errors to HTTP status codes and response shapes is a presentation/transport job. It is also inline low-level infrastructure work: password checks with bcrypt.compare, session-hash creation with crypto.createHash('sha256').update(randomStringGenerator()).digest('hex'), and direct JWT signing and verifying with secrets read from ConfigService (getTokensData, register, confirmEmail, forgotPassword, resetPassword, update). These belong behind infrastructure ports (password hasher, token issuer). The HTTP coupling is the clearest misplaced responsibility, so the unit fails.
violation_messages: Transport concern in the application layer: methods such as validateLogin, validateSocialLogin, confirmEmail, confirmNewEmail, forgotPassword, resetPassword, update and refreshToken throw NestJS HTTP exceptions (UnprocessableEntityException, NotFoundException, UnauthorizedException) with HttpStatus codes embedded in the payloads. Mapping errors to HTTP is a presentation/transport job. | Infrastructure concern in the application layer: bcrypt.compare password checks (validateLogin, update), crypto.createHash('sha256') session-hash creation (validateLogin, validateSocialLogin, refreshToken), and direct JWT signing/verifying with config-held secrets (getTokensData, register, confirmEmail, confirmNewEmail, forgotPassword, resetPassword, update). These belong behind infrastructure adapters.

rationale: The file is a DTO in the application layer. It only declares the shape of the input (password, hash) and adds the usual input-validation and API-documentation decorators. It contains no persistence, transport handling, framework logic or business rules beyond declaring the input contract. In NestJS, DTO classes with Swagger and class-validator decorators are the normal way to write application-layer input contracts.

This file only declares a type for the JWT refresh-token payload. It has sessionId, hash, iat and exp, and the first two are taken from the Session domain type. That matches its place under strategies/ in the infrastructure layer, because it describes the transport/auth token structure that the Passport JWT refresh strategy uses. The file has no business rules, no persistence logic and no presentation logic, so every responsibility it has belongs to the infrastructure layer. The import from the domain layer is a dependency-direction question, which is out of scope for this rule.

The file sits in the infrastructure layer (it matches **/*.repository.ts and an infrastructure path). Everything it does is persistence work. It adapts a Mongoose Model to the FileRepository port. In create, findById and findByIds it saves documents, runs queries and maps the results to the domain FileType through FileMapper. It contains no business rules, validation, policy decisions, transport handling or presentation logic. All of its responsibilities fit an infrastructure repository adapter.

The file is declared domain because its name matches the **/*.entity.ts pattern. Its only job, though, is a TypeORM table mapping. `@Entity({ name: 'file' })` maps the class to a database table. `@PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid')` and `@Column()` define the database schema. The class also extends `EntityRelationalHelper`, a helper for relational storage. That is persistence, which belongs to the infrastructure layer. The file holds no domain behaviour or business rules. Its path (src/files/infrastructure/persistence/relational/entities) shows it is meant as an infrastructure persistence model. The files that use it, a repository, a mapper and the persistence module, support that. Judged against its declared domain layer, it holds a misplaced persistence responsibility. The likely fix is to classify it as infrastructure; it does not need to be rewritten.
violation_messages: `FileEntity` is declared domain but does persistence work. `@Entity({ name: 'file' })`, `@PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid')` and `@Column()` define a database table, and the class extends the relational helper `EntityRelationalHelper`. This belongs to the infrastructure layer, not domain.

rationale: This file is declared presentation because it matches **/*.module.ts. A Nest module can fairly act as a composition root that wires infrastructure, so this could be read as framework wiring. But inside the MulterModule.registerAsync useFactory, the file writes three behaviours inline instead of delegating them: (1) a fileFilter that sets which file types may be uploaded (jpg/jpeg/png/gif only) and rejects others with an UnprocessableEntityException. This is an upload policy or business rule, which belongs in the application or domain layer, or in a dedicated validator. (2) diskStorage with a hardcoded destination './files'. This is persistence and storage logic, which belongs in an infrastructure adapter. (3) The diskStorage filename callback, which builds stored file names from randomStringGenerator() and the lower-cased original extension. This is also storage logic for the infrastructure layer. The module also picks the persistence module at load time by calling databaseConfig().isDocumentDatabase. That is acceptable wiring. The inline policy and storage code is not, so the file holds responsibilities from more than one layer.
violation_messages: The fileFilter in MulterModule.registerAsync useFactory puts the allowed upload file types (jpg/jpeg/png/gif) and the rejection policy inline in a presentation module. This upload rule belongs in the application or domain layer, or in a dedicated validator. | diskStorage({ destination: './files', filename: ... }) puts local disk persistence and file-naming logic inline in a presentation module. This storage logic belongs in an infrastructure adapter.

rationale: The file is declared as an application-layer service because it matches **/*.service.ts. Some of what it does fits that layer: it checks that a file was supplied and it persists the record through FileRepository. But it also handles HTTP transport work that belongs to the presentation layer. It builds an HTTP error response with a status code and an error body. It takes the Express/Multer upload object as its input type. It also builds a public URL from the configured API prefix and the API version. Because these transport and framework concerns sit inside an application-layer unit, the rule fails. Confidence is moderate because putting HTTP exceptions in services is a common NestJS habit.
violation_messages: FilesLocalService.create() throws UnprocessableEntityException with HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY and an HTTP error body. Building an HTTP response belongs to the presentation layer, not this application-layer service. | FilesLocalService.create() takes an Express.Multer.File and builds the stored path from the API prefix and '/v1/' (`/${apiPrefix}/v1/${file.path}`). Handling the framework upload object and building routing URLs are transport concerns that belong to the presentation layer.

rationale: src/mailer/mailer.service.ts is placed in the application layer because of its *.service.ts suffix, but it contains no use-case or orchestration logic. It works only as a technical adapter. It builds and owns an SMTP transport with nodemailer, configured from the connection settings (host, port, TLS and auth credentials). It reads template files from disk with node:fs/promises, compiles them with Handlebars, and sends mail over SMTP. Talking to an external transport, reading the file system and rendering templates are infrastructure work. The application-level orchestration lives in MailService (src/mail/mail.service.ts), which injects this class as a dependency. So this file takes on infrastructure work while declared as application.
violation_messages: MailerService is declared as application layer but does infrastructure work. Its constructor sets up the SMTP transport (nodemailer.createTransport with host, port, TLS and auth settings). sendMail reads from the file system (fs.readFile), renders templates (Handlebars.compile) and sends over SMTP (transporter.sendMail). These belong in an infrastructure adapter, for example src/infrastructure/mailer, behind a port that the application layer uses.

rationale: The file is assigned to the domain layer because it matches the **/*.entity.ts pattern. Everything it does is relational persistence mapping, though. The RoleEntity class is a TypeORM ORM model: it maps to a table, defines its columns and extends a relational helper. A domain file should not carry persistence or framework concerns, so the file fails the rubric as written. The file's path (src/roles/infrastructure/persistence/relational/entities/) shows it was meant to be infrastructure, so the likely cause is a wrong layer assignment from the *.entity.ts pattern. The usual fix is to reclassify the file as infrastructure, or to narrow the domain pattern so it skips infrastructure/persistence paths. Rewriting the file is probably not needed.
violation_messages: The class RoleEntity is declared in the domain layer but carries TypeORM persistence mapping (@Entity({ name: 'role' }), @PrimaryColumn id, @Column name, extends EntityRelationalHelper). That responsibility belongs to the infrastructure layer kind. Reclassify the file as infrastructure, or keep a framework-free domain Role model separate from this ORM entity.

rationale: The file passes. SessionRelationalRepository is an infrastructure persistence adapter. It implements the SessionRepository port, and its only job is persistence: it runs TypeORM queries (findOne, save, create, update, softDelete) and uses SessionMapper to convert between persistence entities and domain objects. It holds no transport, presentation or business-rule logic. Two things looked like possible rule violations, but neither is one. In updateByHash, the hash condition and the check on `affected` are persistence-level concurrency checks. In update, throwing 'Session not found' is a lookup guard, not a domain policy. Both fit the infrastructure role.

This file is an abstract repository class. It only declares persistence operations on Session: finding, creating, updating, updating by hash and deleting. It has no implementation and no business rules, and it contains no transport or framework logic. A persistence contract like this belongs in the infrastructure layer. Some designs put this kind of port in the domain or application layer instead, but having it in infrastructure does not give the file a responsibility from another layer kind. Import direction is out of scope for this rule.

The file is declared domain only because it matches the `**/*.entity.ts` pattern. Its only responsibility is mapping to a relational table with TypeORM: `@Entity({ name: 'status' })` names the table, `@PrimaryColumn` and `@Column` map the columns, and the class extends `EntityRelationalHelper`, a relational persistence helper. It holds no business rules or domain behaviour. Persistence mapping belongs to the infrastructure layer. The path (`infrastructure/persistence/relational/entities`) also suggests the layer model may be classifying this file wrongly. Judged against its declared domain layer, the file carries persistence work, so it fails.
violation_messages: Class StatusEntity is declared domain but carries persistence work: `@Entity({ name: 'status' })`, `@PrimaryColumn()`/`@Column()` TypeORM mappings, and it extends EntityRelationalHelper. This belongs to the infrastructure layer, not the domain layer.

rationale: src/users/domain/user.ts is declared as a domain file, but it does work that belongs to other layers. When the module loads, it reads the database configuration (databaseConfig().isDocumentDatabase) to choose the id type, which is a persistence/infrastructure concern. Every field also carries Swagger @ApiProperty metadata, which is transport/API documentation for the presentation layer. It also uses class-transformer @Expose/@Exclude with response groups ('me', 'admin'), which is presentation logic: it decides which fields go into API responses for each audience. A domain entity should hold domain state and rules without depending on the database driver or HTTP serialization.
violation_messages: The module-level `idType` statement calls databaseConfig() and branches on isDocumentDatabase. This puts persistence/infrastructure configuration logic in the domain entity. | The User class fields carry @ApiProperty Swagger decorators, which are presentation/transport API-documentation metadata, inside the domain layer. | The User class uses class-transformer @Expose({ groups: ['me','admin'] }) and @Exclude({ toPlainOnly: true }) to control response serialization. This is a presentation concern inside the domain entity.

rationale: src/users/dto/user.dto.ts holds one DTO, UserDto. It has a single `id` field with a Swagger @ApiProperty annotation and a class-validator @IsNotEmpty constraint. That is a plain data contract with input validation, which is the normal job of a DTO in the application layer. The file has no persistence code, no transport handling, no business rules and no framework wiring. Declarative Swagger and validation annotations are the usual way NestJS DTOs are written, and they don't add a responsibility from another layer.

The file is assigned to the domain layer because it matches the `**/*.entity.ts` pattern. Its content is entirely relational persistence mapping. The `UserEntity` class is a TypeORM table mapping: it declares the table name, columns, indexes, relations with eager loading and join columns, and soft-delete and timestamp columns. It also extends `EntityRelationalHelper`. This is persistence logic, which belongs to the infrastructure layer, not domain. The file's path (`src/users/infrastructure/persistence/relational/...`) and the mappers that convert it to a domain model confirm it is an infrastructure persistence model. Under the declared domain layer, this is a misplaced persistence responsibility. The root cause is probably that the `**/*.entity.ts` pattern classifies this file wrongly. Either way, measured against the domain role, the file fails.
violation_messages: `UserEntity` is declared in the domain layer but is a TypeORM persistence mapping. It uses `@Entity({ name: 'user' })`, `@Column`, `@Index`, `@ManyToOne` and `@OneToOne` with `eager`, `@JoinColumn`, the `@CreateDateColumn`/`@UpdateDateColumn`/`@DeleteDateColumn` decorators, and `extends EntityRelationalHelper`. These are table, column and relation mapping concerns that belong to the infrastructure (persistence) layer, not domain.

rationale: The file is assigned to the presentation layer by the **/*.module.ts pattern. In this layer model, NestJS module files are where dependency-injection wiring lives. RelationalUserPersistenceModule only declares that wiring: it registers UserEntity with TypeOrmModule.forFeature, binds the abstract UserRepository token to the UsersRelationalRepository class, and exports that token. The file contains no business rules, no query or persistence logic, and no request or transport handling. The real persistence work stays in the repository classes, which are in the infrastructure layer. The folder path is under infrastructure/persistence, but the declared layer comes from the *.module.ts pattern, and the module wiring fits the role the model gives to module files. No ADR prose was provided to contradict this.

This file is a TypeORM repository adapter in the infrastructure layer. Every method handles persistence. Each one builds TypeORM query options (where, skip/take, order, In), calls the TypeORM Repository (find, findOne, save, create, softDelete) and maps between the persistence entity and the domain model through UserMapper. The pagination offset math, the role filter and the sort-order reduce turn query parameters into a database query, which is normal infrastructure work. The early null returns in findByEmail and findBySocialIdAndProvider are defensive guards, not business rules. The 'User not found' error in update is a basic persistence failure, not a domain decision. The file has no transport, presentation or business-rule logic.

The file is a NestJS interceptor. Its layer is presentation, matched by the **/*.interceptor.ts pattern. It does one thing: it takes the response observable in intercept() and resolves any nested promises before the response is serialized. That is response-pipeline and framework work, which belongs in presentation. There are no business rules, no persistence and no domain logic in it.

The module is about one concern: access grants. access.module.ts wires AccessController and AccessService together with the Configuration and Prisma modules. The controller gets its data through AccessService (accesses, access, createAccess, deleteAccess, updateAccess), so Prisma is never used directly. The unit still fails the rubric's duplication criterion because two access policies are copied across handlers. (1) The subscription rule (ENABLE_FEATURE_SUBSCRIPTION && subscription.type === 'Basic' means 403) appears word for word in both createAccess and updateAccess. (2) The ownership rule (accessService.access({ id, userId: request.user.id }) and 403 if it is missing) is repeated in deleteAccess and updateAccess. These are domain or authorization rules that should each live in one place, such as a guard, a helper or a service method. Instead they are rebuilt in several controller methods, so changes to one copy may not reach the others. The judgment is moderately uncertain because the duplication is all inside one file and the pattern is common in NestJS controllers.
violation_messages: The subscription rule (ENABLE_FEATURE_SUBSCRIPTION && subscription.type === 'Basic' means 403 FORBIDDEN) is duplicated in createAccess and updateAccess instead of living in one place (for example a guard, a helper or a service method). | The ownership rule (accessService.access({ id, userId: request.user.id }) and 403 if missing) is duplicated in deleteAccess and updateAccess instead of being kept in one place, such as an AccessService method or a guard.

rationale: Both files deal with one thing: admin control over background job queues. queue.module.ts wires QueueController and QueueService together and imports the three queue modules (DataGatheringQueueModule, PortfolioSnapshotQueueModule, StatisticsGatheringQueueModule) that the service needs. queue.controller.ts exposes job endpoints under 'admin/queue' (deleteJobs, getJobs, deleteJob, executeJob). Every one of those endpoints passes its work to the injected QueueService, so the controller never goes around the module's own service to reach Bull queues directly. Every endpoint also uses the same permission check (@HasPermission(permissions.accessAdminControl) with AuthGuard('jwt') and HasPermissionGuard). Repeating these decorators on each method is normal NestJS practice, not a duplicated invariant. There is one small repeat: deleteJobs and getJobs both turn the status query string into a list with the same line, `filterByStatus?.split(',') as JobStatus[]`. It is trivial input parsing inside one controller, not a business rule split across files, so it doesn't amount to a cohesion failure.

Both files cover market-data endpoints. market-data.module.ts only wires up MarketDataController and the modules that supply the services it injects (AdminModule, MarketDataServiceModule, SymbolModule, SymbolProfileModule and the two TransformDataSource interceptor modules). It holds no logic. The controller has three handlers on the 'market-data' route: getMarketDataOfMarkets, getMarketDataBySymbol and updateMarketData. Each one passes the work to an injected service (symbolService.get, adminService.getMarketDataBySymbol, marketDataService.updateMany) and never reaches past the module's dependencies. The data-source interceptors and the jwt AuthGuard are used consistently. The controller checks permissions inline with hasPermission() and does not use the HasPermission decorator for the two symbol routes. That is justified because those checks depend on whether the asset profile belongs to the current user, which the guard can't express, so it doesn't bypass the module's tools. One weakness: getMarketDataBySymbol and updateMarketData repeat the same steps. Both call getSymbolProfiles([{ dataSource, symbol }]) and then run the check `!assetProfile && !isCurrency(getCurrencyFromSymbol(symbol))` → 404. A private helper would be cleaner. The repeat is two handlers in one file, the permission logic differs (read vs create+update), and the rule is not spread across files. So it doesn't amount to a failure.

SitemapService covers one concern, building sitemap XML. However, the rule for turning a tagged route segment into translated text is written twice. createRouteSitemapUrl is the service's own way to do it: it matches TRANSLATION_TAGGED_MESSAGE_REGEX, calls i18nService.getTranslation and falls back to the original text (match.groups.message). getPersonalFinanceTools skips this and repeats the regex match and getTranslation call three times (resources, personal-finance-tools and product paths). It then passes the already-translated text into createRouteSitemapUrl, so that function's translation step does nothing. The copies don't have the fallback, so the two paths behave differently: if a translation is missing, the value is null and the later link.match call throws. This counts as a duplicated, inconsistent rule that should live in one place, so the unit fails, with moderate confidence. The file is otherwise cohesive, and the product segment adds an alias, so those paths can't be passed in unchanged.
violation_messages: getPersonalFinanceTools repeats the tagged-segment translation (TRANSLATION_TAGGED_MESSAGE_REGEX + i18nService.getTranslation) three times instead of using createRouteSitemapUrl, which already does it. The copies drop the '?? match.groups.message' fallback, so the same rule behaves differently in two places.

rationale: The unit passes. It is a single file, src/app/logo/logo.service.ts, and it handles one concern: getting logo image buffers. Both public entry points send their work through the same private helper, getBuffer, so the favicon-provider URL, the User-Agent header and the timeout are each set in one place. The service gets asset profiles through the injected SymbolProfileService and the timeout through the injected ConfigurationService, so it does not bypass the module's own abstractions. The not-found HttpException is built twice in getLogoByDataSourceAndSymbol. That is a small local repetition of an error response, not a business rule or invariant duplicated across files, so it does not fail the rubric.

The unit has one file, src/app/platform/platform.service.ts, and it deals with a single concern: persisting the Platform entity. Its methods (createPlatform, deletePlatform, getPlatform, getPlatforms, getPlatformsWithAccountCount, updatePlatform) all work on Platform, and every one of them goes through the injected PrismaService (this.prismaService.platform). The file never sidesteps that abstraction and never mixes in unrelated concerns. No rule or invariant is repeated within the unit. The account-count mapping in getPlatformsWithAccountCount exists in only one place. The file passes the cohesion rubric.

The unit has one file, src/app/redis-cache/redis-cache.service.ts, and it handles one concern: the application's Redis cache. It wraps the cache (get, set, remove, reset, getKeys), checks the cache's health (isHealthy) and builds cache keys (getPortfolioSnapshotKey, getQuoteKey). The file is consistent with its own abstractions. isHealthy goes through the service's own set/get/remove methods rather than calling the store directly. removePortfolioSnapshotsByUserId gets its key prefix from getPortfolioSnapshotKey instead of rebuilding the 'portfolio-snapshot-' string. The default-TTL rule lives in one place, inside set. Each key format (portfolio snapshot, quote) is also defined only once. This is the opposite of duplication: it gives the incoming callers one source of truth for key formats. Some might object that the key builders bring portfolio and quote knowledge into a generic cache service. But they are only about how cache keys are named, and keeping them together here adds to cohesion rather than splitting the module. getKeys reads the underlying Keyv client through its iterator because the Cache abstraction has no way to list keys. That fills a gap rather than bypassing the abstraction. I found no split, duplication or bypass.

The unit has one file, src/app/redis-cache/redis-cache.module.ts, and it does one job: it wires up the Redis-backed cache. It registers CacheModule with a factory that builds the Keyv Redis store, then provides and exports RedisCacheService. Every setting (REDIS_PASSWORD, REDIS_HOST, REDIS_PORT, REDIS_DB, CACHE_TTL) is read through ConfigurationService rather than directly from process.env, so the module's own configuration abstraction is not bypassed. The Redis connection URL is built in one place only, inside the useFactory, so no rule or invariant is duplicated within this unit. Whether other modules rebuild the same URL can't be checked from the material provided. Layer and import direction are out of scope.

Both files deal with one concern, performance logging, but they don't use the module's own way of supplying the logging service consistently. PerformanceLoggingModule registers and exports PerformanceLoggingInterceptor and PerformanceLoggingService through Nest dependency injection, and the interceptor gets the service through its constructor. The LogPerformance decorator in the same file instead creates its own copy with `new PerformanceLoggingService()` on every call, so it never uses the module's instance. Any configuration or dependencies the module's copy gets won't reach decorated methods. The decorator is exported from this file, and five of its seven importers are not the module (four services and portfolio-calculator.ts), so the bypass is used widely. The timing and logging steps (startTime via performance.now(), then logPerformance with className, methodName and startTime) are also written out three times: once in intercept and twice in LogPerformance, in separate async and sync branches. There is no shared helper. A Nest decorator can't easily use the module's providers, so this is partly a practical workaround, which keeps confidence moderate. Under this rubric it still counts as bypassing the module's abstractions and duplicating its logic.
violation_messages: The LogPerformance decorator creates its own PerformanceLoggingService with `new PerformanceLoggingService()` on each call instead of using the instance PerformanceLoggingModule provides, which PerformanceLoggingInterceptor gets through its constructor. The file therefore uses two different ways to get the service. | The timing and logging steps (performance.now() for startTime, then logPerformance({ className, methodName, startTime })) are repeated in intercept and in both the async and sync branches of LogPerformance. They should be moved into one shared helper.

rationale: This module has one job: removing sensitive values from HTTP responses for viewers with restricted access. The interceptor file holds all of the logic. It does not write its own permission checks or redaction code. It calls the shared helpers `hasReadRestrictedAccessPermission`, `isRestrictedView` and `redactPaths`, and reads the shared constant `DEFAULT_REDACTED_PATHS`. So the rule for when and what to redact is defined in one place. The module file is an empty NestJS wrapper (`@Module({})`) that lets feature modules import this one. It adds no competing behaviour and goes around nothing. The rule is not broken: the module serves one concern, uses its abstractions consistently, and repeats no rule.

The unit has one file, src/models/rule.ts, which declares one abstract base class, Rule<T extends RuleSettings>. Every member serves one concern: the shared base for portfolio report rules. That covers rule identity (getKey), localization (getLanguageCode), the abstract evaluation methods (evaluate, getConfiguration, getName, getSettings) and a shared helper, groupCurrentHoldingsByAttribute. The incoming graph shows many rule subclasses extend Rule, so the grouping helper lives in this one base class rather than being copied into each rule. The file uses its own abstractions consistently: it implements RuleInterface<T> and returns EvaluationResult. It also delegates currency conversion to the injected exchangeRateDataService.toCurrency instead of computing conversions itself. Nothing in the file splits into unrelated concerns, duplicates a rule, or works around the module's abstractions. The domain-layer Rule depending on the application-layer ExchangeRateDataService is an import-direction question, which is out of scope here.

Both files cover one concern: the contract for portfolio rules and the results they return. RuleInterface<T extends RuleSettings> says evaluate returns an EvaluationResult. It uses the module's own EvaluationResult type and does not redefine that shape inline. Each file declares a single interface, so nothing is repeated, no rule or invariant appears twice, and nothing goes around the module's abstractions. Import direction is out of scope for this review.

Both files cover one concern: X-ray rules that judge account-cluster risk from PortfolioDetails['accounts']. Each extends the shared Rule base class the same way. Each passes ExchangeRateDataService to super, builds its key from its class name, and gets the language code through getLanguageCode() and its settings key through getKey(). Each implements the same set of methods (evaluate, getConfiguration, getName, getSettings), and both translate messages the same way, through i18nService.getTranslation with ids under 'rule.accountClusterRisk*'. Neither file works around the Rule abstraction. Each file owns its own rule logic: the largest-account investment-ratio threshold lives only in current-investment.ts, and the single-account count check lives only in single-account.ts. Some boilerplate repeats: both return false with a '.false.invalid' message when there are no accounts, and both default isActive to true. That is the per-rule pattern the Rule contract asks for, not a shared invariant copied out of its proper home.

Both files serve one cohesive concern (asset-class concentration risk rules) and both use the Rule base-class abstractions consistently. However, the threshold rule itself is copied in full across the two files. evaluate() repeats the same logic: group holdings by 'assetClass', sum the total, compute the ratio, compare against thresholdMax and thresholdMin, and format percentages with toPrecision(3). getConfiguration() returns the same threshold config, the getSettings() shape is the same, and so is the local Settings interface. Only the asset-class key ('EQUITY' vs 'FIXED_INCOME'), the i18n ids and the default thresholds differ. The ratio and threshold check should live in one place, such as a shared base class or helper parameterized by asset class and defaults. Keeping it in two places means a change to the comparison or the config has to be made twice. This matches the rubric's fail condition of duplicating a rule that should live in one place.
violation_messages: evaluate(), getConfiguration() and the Settings interface copy the asset-class ratio/threshold rule that is also in fixed-income.ts, rather than sharing one parameterized implementation. | evaluate(), getConfiguration() and the Settings interface are a near-verbatim copy of equity.ts (only 'FIXED_INCOME', the i18n ids and the defaults differ), so the same threshold rule exists in two places.

rationale: Both files cover one concern: currency concentration risk on current holdings. Each defines a rule class that extends the shared Rule<Settings> abstraction and has the same structure (evaluate, getConfiguration, getName, getSettings). Both group holdings through the inherited groupCurrentHoldingsByAttribute and use I18nService for evaluation text, so neither bypasses the module's abstractions. Each file has its own rule: the base-currency rule checks whether the base currency is the largest group, and the current-investment rule checks whether any currency goes over thresholdMax. The repeated parts (the loop that totals groups and finds the largest, and the isActive default in getSettings) are the standard boilerplate every rule follows, not a business rule written in two places. One minor inconsistency: base-currency-current-investment.ts picks the largest group by 'investment' but computes its ratio from 'value'. That may be a correctness issue but does not break the module's structure.

Both files cover one concern: rules that judge what share of the portfolio sits in a market cluster. Both extend Rule<Settings> and use I18nService and the Rule key and language helpers the same way, so the module's shared abstractions are not bypassed. But the core threshold-band logic is copied word for word into each file instead of being kept in one place: - The ratio is computed as value / currentValueInBaseCurrency, falling back to 0. - The ratio is checked against thresholdMax first, then thresholdMin. - Percentages are formatted with (x * 100).toPrecision(3). - The getConfiguration() threshold bounds are max 1, min 0, step 0.01, unit '%'. - The Settings interface is declared the same way in both files. The only real differences are the translation-key prefix, the field name and the default thresholds (0.68–0.72 vs 0.28–0.32). Any change to how a band is evaluated, rounded or configured would have to be made in both files, which is the "duplicate a rule or invariant that should live in one place" case in the rubric. Confidence is moderate because this one-class-per-rule pattern may be a convention across the wider project.
violation_messages: EconomicMarketClusterRiskDevelopedMarkets.evaluate, getConfiguration and the Settings interface repeat the threshold-band evaluation, percentage formatting and configuration word for word from emerging-markets.ts instead of sharing one implementation. | EconomicMarketClusterRiskEmergingMarkets.evaluate, getConfiguration and the Settings interface repeat the threshold-band evaluation, percentage formatting and configuration word for word from developed-markets.ts instead of sharing one implementation.

rationale: The module has one concern: regional market cluster risk rules. All five rule classes extend Rule<Settings> and share the Settings interface, so the files are cohesive and use the module's abstractions consistently. The problem is duplication. The same threshold-band invariant is copied in full into five files. Each copy computes the region ratio with the same divide-by-zero guard, checks it against thresholdMax and thresholdMin, and formats the results as percentages with toPrecision(3). getConfiguration is also identical in every file (max 1, min 0, step 0.01, unit '%'), and so is the getSettings logic. The only real differences are the region key/translation id, the region value field, and the default thresholds. Any change to the evaluation logic, number formatting or configuration bounds must be made in five places. That fails the rubric's requirement to keep each rule or invariant in one place.
violation_messages: evaluate(), getConfiguration() and getSettings() copy the threshold-band rule, percentage formatting and configuration bounds that the other region rules also contain. This should live in one shared base or parameterized rule. | Duplicates the same ratio/threshold-band evaluation, getConfiguration literal and getSettings logic; only the region key and defaults differ. | Duplicates the same ratio/threshold-band evaluation, getConfiguration literal and getSettings logic; only the region key and defaults differ. | Duplicates the same ratio/threshold-band evaluation, getConfiguration literal and getSettings logic; only the region key and defaults differ. | Duplicates the same ratio/threshold-band evaluation, getConfiguration literal and getSettings logic; only the region key and defaults differ.

rationale: Both unit files serve the single concern of wrapping Alpha Vantage as a data provider. alpha-vantage.service.ts declares AlphaVantageService, which implements DataProviderInterface and OnModuleInit. Every method either calls the Alpha Vantage client or returns a stub required by the interface. interfaces/interfaces.ts declares only AlphaVantageHistoricalResponse, which the service uses solely to type the crypto.daily response. No unrelated concern, duplicated rule or bypassed abstraction was found; the service reuses getName() and getDataProviderInfo() internally rather than repeating that metadata. Two small issues do not amount to a violation. The interface is empty, so the code indexes into it with raw string keys; that is a typing-precision problem, not a cohesion problem. DataSource.ALPHA_VANTAGE appears in both getName() and getDataProviderInfo(), but it is only the identifier the interface requires, not a business rule.

Both files hold contracts for the data-provider subsystem. data-provider.interface.ts defines what a market-data provider must implement (DataProviderInterface) along with its request parameter types. data-enhancer.interface.ts defines the contract for enhancers that add to an asset profile (DataEnhancerInterface). That is one concern: pluggable sources of market data and asset profiles. The two interfaces follow the same conventions: getName() and getTestSymbol(), an optional requestTimeout, object-destructured parameters, and Partial<SymbolProfile> as the asset-profile type. Neither file contains logic, so no business rule is repeated across them. Two small things don't amount to a failure. GetDividendsParams and GetHistoricalParams have identical fields, which is repeated type shape rather than a repeated rule. DataEnhancerInterface.enhance declares its parameter type inline instead of as a named Params interface, which is a small style difference.

This module handles a single concern: checking whether a request may act as another user (an "impersonation id"). The module file only wires the service and its Prisma dependency into NestJS. The service holds the one rule for impersonation in a single method. Nothing in the two files repeats that rule, and neither file goes around the module's own abstractions. The service queries the database through the injected PrismaService and checks permissions with the shared helpers, which fits the project's usual patterns.

The file is a presentation-layer controller, but it holds business rules and builds persistence queries. It enforces a subscription rule: when ENABLE_FEATURE_SUBSCRIPTION is on, Basic users cannot create or update access. It also enforces ownership: an access is only changed if it belongs to the requesting user. It builds Prisma query and relation objects directly (include, orderBy, where, connect, disconnect). It also decides whether an access is PUBLIC or PRIVATE. These belong in the application, domain or infrastructure layers, not presentation. Routing, guards, request binding and turning errors into HTTP responses are fine for a presentation file.
violation_messages: createAccess and updateAccess enforce a subscription rule (when ENABLE_FEATURE_SUBSCRIPTION is on, Basic users get FORBIDDEN). This business rule belongs in the application/domain layer, not presentation. | deleteAccess and updateAccess enforce an ownership check (accessService.access({ id, userId }) followed by FORBIDDEN when nothing is found). This application-level authorization rule should live in AccessService. | getAllAccesses, createAccess and updateAccess build Prisma query and relation objects (include, orderBy, where, connect, disconnect). Persistence query construction belongs in infrastructure or the service, not the controller. | The getAllAccesses map labels an access PUBLIC or PRIVATE (grantee 'Public') depending on whether it has a grantee user. This is domain/application logic placed in presentation.

rationale: The controller does normal presentation-layer work. It declares routes (@Controller, @Post, @Delete), applies auth and permission guards, binds the request body and route params, and maps a missing resource to an HTTP 403 via HttpException. Everything else is passed to application services (AccountService, AccountBalanceService). It contains no direct persistence calls, no domain calculations and no business rules beyond a request-scoped ownership check. That check is just a lookup scoped by userId, and placing it in the controller is acceptable access control at the transport boundary. One minor point: the Prisma composite-key filter shape (`id_userId`) is passed through accountService.account(), which leaks a persistence-shaped query detail into the controller. But this is a parameter to a service call, not persistence logic run by the controller, so it does not amount to a misplaced responsibility under this rubric.

ActivitiesService is in the application layer, so it should orchestrate use cases: coordinate services, emit events and enqueue jobs. Much of the file does that. But it also contains a lot of persistence logic, which belongs to the infrastructure layer. It calls the Prisma ORM client directly (`prismaService.order.findMany/create/update/delete/deleteMany/count/aggregate/findUnique`). It also builds complex, database-specific queries: in getActivities it assembles `Prisma.OrderWhereInput` filters, including case-insensitive `startsWith` matching, null checks on `SymbolProfileOverrides`, and the `orderBy` list. It reshapes ORM write inputs by mutating `connectOrCreate` and `connect` and deleting fields before writing. The private `orders()` method is a plain repository-style wrapper around `findMany`. None of this goes through a repository or other infrastructure abstraction, so the file carries infrastructure (persistence) responsibilities that the layer model assigns elsewhere, for example to `*.repository.ts`.
violation_messages: getActivities() builds complex, database-specific Prisma.OrderWhereInput and orderBy clauses (case-insensitive startsWith matching, SymbolProfileOverrides null checks) and runs prismaService.order.count. That is persistence query logic, which belongs to the infrastructure layer (a repository), not the application layer. | The private orders() method and getStatisticsByCurrency() call prismaService.order.findMany and prismaService.order.aggregate directly. These are repository/data-access responsibilities that belong to the infrastructure layer. | createActivity(), updateActivity(), deleteActivity(), deleteActivities() and assignTags() reshape Prisma ORM inputs (connectOrCreate, connect, tags set/connect) and call prismaService.order.create/update/delete/deleteMany directly. These ORM persistence details belong to the infrastructure layer.

rationale: AdminController sits in the presentation layer. Most of its handlers do presentation work: routing, guards and permission decorators, reading parameters, sanitising input (isNaN on skip/take, parseISO on dateString), turning errors into HTTP responses, and passing calls on to services. Three handlers go further than that. 1. gatherMax and gatherProfileData build queue jobs themselves. Each one fetches the active asset profiles, maps them to job payloads, picks the job name, merges the job options, sets the jobId and chooses a queue priority, then submits the batch. gatherProfileDataForSymbol does the same for one symbol, with its own priority. Choosing priorities and assembling jobs is application-level orchestration. It belongs in DataGatheringService or another application service. The same logic is copied into two handlers, which also suggests it is not presentation work. 2. testMarketData treats a falsy price as a failure and raises an error with a domain message. This is a smaller issue. Translating a date range into a start date in gatherSymbol counts as input translation, so I did not flag it.
violation_messages: gatherMax() and gatherProfileData() each build queue job payloads in the controller: job name, merged options, jobId from getAssetProfileIdentifier and priority DATA_GATHERING_QUEUE_PRIORITY_MEDIUM. The same logic appears in both. This is application-layer orchestration and belongs in DataGatheringService or another application service. | gatherProfileDataForSymbol() builds a queue job in the controller, including the choice of DATA_GATHERING_QUEUE_PRIORITY_HIGH and the jobId. Choosing queue priority and assembling jobs is application-layer work.

rationale: AuthController does presentation work only. It declares HTTP routes, attaches guards (passport AuthGuard, HasPermissionGuard), reads request bodies and params, and passes the real work to AuthService and WebAuthService. It turns service errors into HTTP 403 responses and sends OAuth callbacks to a frontend URL. Building that redirect URL from ROOT_URL and the language code is transport or routing work, not a business rule. The ENABLE_FEATURE_AUTH_OIDC check in oidcLogin is a feature flag that blocks an endpoint, which is also an ordinary transport-level concern. Login validation, WebAuthn verification and token issuing all happen in the services. The file has no persistence code and no domain logic.

This file belongs to the application layer. Most of what it does fits that role: it coordinates several data providers, merges their results, derives currency quotes, filters and sorts lookup results, and reports status. However, two methods build Prisma queries directly against specific tables: an upsert into assetProfileResolution with a compound unique key and an increment, and an increment on analytics.dataProviderGhostfolioDailyRequests. Building ORM queries like this is persistence work, which belongs in the infrastructure layer (a repository or adapter). An application service should call that layer through an abstraction rather than build table-level queries itself. Confidence is moderate because injecting PrismaService straight into services is a common NestJS convention, and the graph labels PrismaService as application.
violation_messages: getAssetProfile() builds an inline Prisma upsert on assetProfileResolution, with a compound unique where-key and a requestCount increment. This is persistence logic and belongs in the infrastructure layer (a repository), not in an application service. | incrementDailyRequests() runs a direct Prisma update on the analytics table (dataProviderGhostfolioDailyRequests increment). This is persistence logic and belongs in the infrastructure layer (a repository), not in an application service.

rationale: The export controller does only presentation-layer work. It defines the HTTP route with @Controller and @Get, applies authentication and permission guards and the request/response interceptors, and binds the query parameters. Its only data handling is turning the comma-separated query strings into arrays with split(','), which is transport-level input parsing. It passes the filter parameters to ApiService.buildFiltersFromQueryParams and hands the actual export to ExportService.export, along with the user id and settings taken from the request. It contains no persistence logic, no business rules and no domain calculations. The @prisma/client import is only used as a type cast. Import direction is out of scope for this check.

The controller only does presentation work. It handles HTTP routing (@Controller, @Get), binds request params and query values, attaches a request interceptor, passes the work to LogoService, and turns the result into an HTTP response (content type, body, or a 404 on error). It has no business rules, no persistence and no outbound fetch logic. The DataSource import from @prisma/client is only used as a type on a route parameter, not for persistence. That is a dependency question, which is out of scope here.

The file holds a single interface, EvaluationResult, with two fields: evaluation (string) and value (boolean). It describes the result of evaluating a rule, which is a domain concept. Only domain files import it (rule.interface.ts and rule.ts). It has no persistence, transport, framework or presentation code, so its only responsibility fits the domain layer.

This file sits in the domain layer, and its main job is domain work: an X-ray business rule that checks whether money is too concentrated in one account. evaluate() adds up each account's investment, finds the largest account, works out its share of the total and compares that share with the user's thresholdMax. getSettings() turns user preferences into rule settings, including the default threshold of 0.5. Both are domain logic. There is no persistence, transport or framework logic here. Account from @prisma/client is used only as a type (Pick<Account, 'name'>). Nothing is stored or fetched, and no HTTP or framework code runs. Building the localized messages is handed off to the injected I18nService, so the file never builds UI strings itself. The explanation message is reasonably part of what a rule evaluation returns. Two small things lean toward presentation: getConfiguration() includes UI hints (step 0.01, unit '%'), and evaluate() formats the percentage with toPrecision(3). Neither is enough to say a whole responsibility has been put in the wrong layer. Whether this file should depend on services from the application layer is an import-direction question, which is out of scope. I'm only moderately confident because the localization and UI-hint parts are a judgment call.

The file's main responsibility is a domain business rule, which fits the domain layer. It groups holdings by asset class, works out what share of the total is fixed income, and checks that share against minimum and maximum thresholds. getSettings() resolves the rule's default thresholds. The file has no persistence, transport or framework controller logic. Some of its output is presentation-style: it returns translated text through I18nService, rounds percentages for display with toPrecision(3), and getConfiguration() returns slider settings (step, unit '%'). That is borderline. It was not counted as a violation because translation is handed off to an injected service, and the message and settings describe the rule itself rather than rendering it. Imports of application services are a dependency-direction issue, which is out of scope.

The file is a domain rule. evaluate() is portfolio business logic: it groups holdings by currency, adds up the total value, finds the group with the largest investment and checks whether that group is the base currency, then computes the base-currency value ratio. getSettings() turns user settings into rule settings, which is rule configuration. The file has no persistence, transport (HTTP) or framework logic. The borderline part is user-facing text: evaluate() and getName() build translated messages through I18nService.getTranslation, and the ratio is formatted with toPrecision(3). That leans toward presentation, but the translation is handed to an injected service and the message only reports the rule's outcome, so I did not treat it as a misplaced responsibility. Injecting application-layer services (ExchangeRateDataService, I18nService) is a dependency-direction question, which is out of scope.

The file holds a portfolio X-Ray rule, which is domain business logic. `evaluate()` works out what share of the portfolio is in emerging markets and checks that share against the minimum and maximum thresholds. `getSettings()` sets the business defaults (0.28 and 0.32) and reads per-user overrides. `getConfiguration()` describes the rule's adjustable threshold range. None of this is persistence, transport or framework logic. The file does no database access, HTTP handling or framework wiring. Two points are borderline: - Formatting: the user-facing evaluation text is built through the injected `I18nService` (the methods call `this.i18nService.getTranslation(...)`), and the percentages are formatted with `toPrecision(3)`. This is close to presentation work, but the file only hands it off to the service. The domain rule still produces the business result in `value`. - UI metadata: `getConfiguration()` returns `step` and `unit` values that look like settings-UI hints. They describe the rule's own adjustable range rather than rendering anything. The file also depends on application services (`ExchangeRateDataService` and `I18nService`). That is an import-direction question, which is out of scope here. Overall, no responsibility clearly belongs to a different layer kind.

The file sits in src/models/** (domain) and holds a portfolio X-ray business rule: it works out a fee ratio and checks it against a configurable maximum threshold. That is domain logic. The file has no persistence, transport, HTTP or framework code. It does not touch a database or an external API. The localized evaluation text is built by calling an injected I18nService. Formatting the percentages for that text is a small part of the job. getConfiguration() returns threshold metadata (min, max, step and unit) that describes the rule's own parameters. getSettings() resolves the rule's settings from user preferences, with defaults. All of these are part of the rule's definition, inherited from the Rule base class. None of them belongs to another layer kind. The domain depending on application services (ExchangeRateDataService and I18nService) is an import-direction concern, which is out of scope here. Building localized messages inside the domain is a borderline presentation concern. It is delegated to a service rather than done in the file, so I do not count it as a misplaced responsibility.

The file's main job fits the domain layer. `evaluate()` works out the share of the portfolio in emerging markets and checks it against the minimum and maximum thresholds. `getSettings()` supplies the default threshold values (0.08 and 0.12). Both are business logic. The file also takes on presentation work. `evaluate()` and `getName()` build user-facing text. They choose translation keys, pass a language code to `I18nService.getTranslation`, and format numbers for display by multiplying by 100 and calling `toPrecision(3)`. The rule's result is a finished message, not just pass/fail plus the ratio. `getConfiguration()` returns settings for a UI control, such as `step: 0.01` and `unit: '%'`, which are presentation details rather than business rules. The dependency on `I18nService` is an import-direction question, which is out of scope here. The verdict rests only on what the code does: it builds the display text and UI settings itself. No ADR prose was provided to justify this. Confidence is moderate because putting human-readable descriptions on domain rules is a common, deliberate design choice.
violation_messages: evaluate() and getName() build user-facing text: they choose translation keys, pass the language code to I18nService.getTranslation and format percentages for display with toPrecision(3). Localizing and formatting display text is presentation work, not domain work. The domain rule should return the evaluation result and the ratio, and leave the wording to the presentation layer. | getConfiguration() returns settings for a UI control (step: 0.01, unit: '%'). These are presentation details, not business rules, and don't belong in a domain rule.

rationale: The file holds one declarative NestJS @Module that sets up dependency injection for BenchmarkService: it registers it as a provider, exports it and imports the modules it depends on. It has no business rules, no persistence queries, no HTTP/transport handling and no other executable logic. It does match the presentation pattern **/*.module.ts, but its declared layer is application (src/services/**). Its only job is to package and expose an application service, which is the standard way to put an application service together in NestJS. Importing PrismaModule and RedisCacheModule is a dependency-direction question, and that is out of scope here. Nothing in the file belongs to a different layer kind.

DataProviderService is declared in the application layer. Most of its work fits that role: it picks a data provider, validates activities, applies subscription and premium rules, and gathers quotes and search results from the providers. One method goes further. getHistorical writes raw SQL against the "MarketData" table and runs it directly through prismaService.$queryRaw. It builds Prisma.sql fragments by hand, including a date_part() granularity filter and ::timestamp casts. Hand-built SQL and direct database access are persistence work, which belongs in an infrastructure repository and not an application service. The same service already uses a MarketDataService abstraction for writes (updateMany) but skips it for this read. getQuotes also handles cache plumbing itself: it builds Redis keys, serializes and parses JSON, and applies the cache TTL. That is closer to infrastructure, but it goes through an injected cache service, so it is a lesser concern. The raw SQL query alone is enough to fail the rule.
violation_messages: getHistorical() builds and runs a raw SQL query against the MarketData table (prismaService.$queryRaw, Prisma.sql/Prisma.join, date_part and ::timestamp casts). This is persistence work for the infrastructure layer, such as a repository or MarketDataService, not an application service.

rationale: YahooFinanceService is declared application (via the *.service.ts pattern under src/services/), but its role is an infrastructure adapter for an external API. It implements DataProviderInterface, which acts as a port. It creates the third-party yahoo-finance2 client itself, calls the vendor API directly (chart, quote, quoteSummary, search) with vendor-specific request parameters, maps vendor response types (ChartResultArray, QuoteResponseArray, QuoteSummaryResult) to internal shapes, and translates vendor error messages into application errors. This is gateway/transport work for the infrastructure layer, not use-case orchestration for the application layer.
violation_messages: The `yahooFinance` field (`new YahooFinance(...)`) and the methods getDividends, getHistorical, getQuotes, search and getQuotesWithQuoteSummary call the external Yahoo Finance API directly (chart/quote/quoteSummary/search), build vendor request parameters and map vendor responses and errors. This is an external-API adapter responsibility that belongs to the infrastructure layer, not the application layer.

rationale: DataGatheringService sits in the application layer. Some of its work fits that layer: it orchestrates gathering jobs, picks queue priorities, chooses which symbols to gather and coordinates data providers and enhancers. But it also writes its own Prisma queries. These include upserts keyed on composite unique keys, groupBy aggregations, findMany calls with select/orderBy/where clauses, and findFirst on orders. That is persistence work, which belongs in the infrastructure layer (repositories). An application service should reach storage through repositories or ports, not build ORM queries itself. Some business filtering is also mixed into these queries, such as excluding 'MANUAL' and 'RAPID_API' data sources and counting 'CLOSE'-state rows. Using the Bull queue directly is borderline transport work, but it could pass as orchestration. The Prisma data access is the clear misplaced responsibility.
violation_messages: gatherSymbolForDate and gatherAssetProfiles run Prisma upserts directly (marketData.upsert, symbolProfile.upsert with composite-key where clauses). This is persistence work that belongs in an infrastructure repository, not in an application service. | getActiveAssetProfileIdentifiers, getAssetProfileIdentifiersWithCompleteMarketData and getSymbolsMax build raw Prisma queries (findMany, groupBy, findFirst with select/orderBy/where). This is infrastructure-layer data access placed in the application layer.

rationale: This file only sets up NestJS dependency injection. The `@Module` decorator imports PrismaModule, registers SymbolProfileService as a provider and exports it. That is how the symbol-profile application service gets packaged so other modules can use it. The file has no business rules, no persistence queries, no transport handling and no presentation logic. Importing PrismaModule makes the database client available to the service. It is not a persistence responsibility carried by this file. The path places the file in the application layer, while the `*.module.ts` pattern maps to presentation. That conflict does not matter here, because packaging and exposing a service is acceptable in either layer, and nothing in the file belongs to another layer kind.

The module has two files that split repository contracts into a read side and a write side, CQRS-style. Together they cover one concern: persistence contracts for aggregate roots. Both interfaces use the same generic parameters with the same constraints (TKey extends Primitives, TDomain extends DddAggregateRoot<any, any>) and import those types from the same shared sources, so the abstractions line up. Neither interface repeats the other's operations. Repeating the generic constraint in both is just a type signature, not a business rule or invariant that ought to live in one place. Neither file goes around the module's abstractions. One small inconsistency: IDomainReadRepository has a JSDoc comment on the interface itself and IDomainWriteRepository doesn't. That's a documentation style point, not a cohesion problem.
