The six files serve one purpose: base value objects (Id, Number, String) and the AbstractRuleValidator subclasses that enforce their rules. They also use the module's abstractions consistently: validators extend AbstractRuleValidator and are registered through validatorRules in addValidators(). The unit fails on the 'duplicate a rule or invariant' criterion. The rule that a number must not be null, undefined, NaN or Infinity belongs to NumberNotNullValidator, which can be configured with allowNaN and allowInfinity. NumberPositiveValidator.addRules() writes its own copy of that rule, and in that copy NaN and Infinity are always rejected. NumberValueObject.addValidators() registers both validators. It passes allowNaN and allowInfinity only to NumberNotNullValidator, and passes only allowZero and epsilon to NumberPositiveValidator. With the default requirePositive=true, the duplicate check overrides the configured options: NumberValueObject.create(Infinity, { allowInfinity: true }) is still rejected, and a NaN value allowed through allowNaN is still rejected. The string side does this correctly. StringMaxLengthValidator.addRules() returns early on null and leaves that rule to StringNotNullOrEmptyValidator. A smaller point: IdValueObject validates UUIDs in two places, assertUuid and UuidFormatValidator, but the code comments explain why (fail fast on input, and keep isValid accurate if the value is later re-checked). I did not count that as a violation.
violation_messages: NumberPositiveValidator.addRules() repeats the null/undefined/NaN/Infinity rule that NumberNotNullValidator owns, and its copy always rejects NaN and Infinity. This copy has already drifted from the configurable one. | addValidators() registers both NumberNotNullValidator and NumberPositiveValidator but passes allowNaN/allowInfinity only to the first. With requirePositive=true (the default), the second validator's own check rejects NaN and Infinity even when the options allow them.

rationale: The unit is a standard CQRS pair. get-orders.query.ts holds the query parameters (status, limit, offset). get-orders.query-handler.ts handles that query: it filters, paginates and maps orders to the shared OrderResponse and OrderItemResponse types from ../dtos. Both files serve the same concern. The handler reads only the query's own fields, and the response types come from the shared DTO module rather than being redefined. Within these two files, no rule or invariant appears twice. The domain-to-DTO mapping is written inline in the handler. If a sibling handler (for example, a get-order-by-id handler) repeats it, that would be duplication, but no such file is visible here, so I can't call it a violation. The direct injection of the concrete infrastructure OrderRepository is a layer-dependency question, which other tools check. I don't count it here.

All four files serve a single concern: cancelling an order. The DTO file defines the input contract (CancelOrderBodyDto, plus CancelOrderDto, which adds orderId). CancelOrderCommand is built only from CancelOrderDto. CancelOrderService turns the DTO into the command and sends it through the CommandBus. CancelOrderCommandHandler loads the order, hands the cancel rule to the domain (order.cancel(reason)), checks the domain's brokenRules, saves and publishes events. Each step uses the module's own abstractions: the service never skips the bus to call the handler or repository, and the handler takes the command rather than the raw DTO. The only input validation is @IsString on reason, and the cancellation rules stay in the domain entity, so nothing is repeated across files. CancelOrderBodyDto is labelled as the HTTP transport contract, but it is a thin base type for this use case's own input and does not split the unit's purpose. The handler's dependency on the concrete infrastructure OrderRepository is a layer-dependency issue, which is out of scope.

All four files cover one concern, the confirm-order use case, and follow the usual CQRS pattern. ConfirmOrderDto holds the input. ConfirmOrderCommand is built from the DTO. ConfirmOrderService sends the command through the CommandBus. ConfirmOrderCommandHandler runs it: it loads the order, calls order.confirm(), checks for broken rules, saves the order and commits events. Each rule or invariant lives in one place: the handler owns the not-found and broken-rules checks, and the command only copies orderId. The service uses the command bus instead of calling the handler or repository directly, so the module's abstractions aren't bypassed. The handler depends on the infrastructure OrderRepository, but that is import direction, which is out of scope.

The unit has one file, src/orders/domain/events/order.events.ts. All of it deals with one concern: immutable domain-event payloads for the Order aggregate's lifecycle (created, item added/removed/quantity changed, confirmed, status changed, cancelled, shipped, delivered). The file contains no business logic, so it cannot duplicate a rule or invariant. Every event identifies the aggregate the same way, with `orderId: IdValueObject`. Status transitions use the module's own OrderStatus enum instead of raw strings. There are minor inconsistencies: `customerId` is a plain string while the order and product ids are IdValueObject, and money is passed as a raw number plus a currency string. These are payload-typing choices, and nothing in the provided material shows that a customer-id or Money value object exists in the module and is being bypassed. They are not enough to fail cohesion or show a bypassed abstraction.

The unit has one file, `src/orders/domain/entities/order-item.entity.ts`. Its concern is coherent: it defines the OrderItem value object. It fails on keeping each rule in one place and on using the module's own abstractions. It checks quantity and product-name rules in its own private static methods (`validateQuantity`, `validateProductName`). It throws `BrokenRulesException` from these and from an inline check in `withIncreasedQuantity`. It also registers `OrderItemQuantityValidator`, `OrderItemProductValidator` and `OrderItemPriceValidator` through the library's `addValidators()`/`validatorRules`. So the same rules are enforced in two places with two different mechanisms, and the hand-written checks go around the validator abstraction the class itself sets up. The file also repeats its own quantity check: `withQuantity` calls `OrderItem.validateQuantity(newQuantity)` and then `OrderItem.create(...)`, which runs `validateQuantity` again. The abstraction is also unclear. The file is named `*.entity.ts` and sits in `entities/`, but the class extends `DddValueObject`. Its doc comment calls it a "Value Object" and its example calls `item.changeQuantity(3)`, a method that doesn't exist; the actual method is `withQuantity`. I haven't seen what the validator classes contain, so the duplication is inferred from their names. That is why confidence is moderate.
violation_messages: The quantity and product-name rules are enforced twice: in the private static methods `validateQuantity` and `validateProductName`, and again by the `OrderItemQuantityValidator` and `OrderItemProductValidator` classes registered in `addValidators()`. The hand-written checks go around the class's own `validatorRules` abstraction. | `withQuantity` runs `validateQuantity` and then calls `create()`, which runs it again. `withIncreasedQuantity` also adds its own inline rule check outside the validator mechanism. | The abstraction is unclear: the file is named and placed as an entity (`*.entity.ts` in `entities/`), but `OrderItem extends DddValueObject` and its doc calls it a value object.

rationale: The three files serve one concern: immutable value objects for the orders domain. All three extend DddValueObject from @nestjslatam/ddd-lib. All three read state through getValue() and define equality through getEqualityComponents(). CustomerInfo and ShippingAddress share one construction pattern: a private constructor, a static create() factory, and a private validateProps() method that throws library exceptions. Money uses factory methods (fromAmount, fromCents, zero) and owns its money rules, such as the cents conversion and the currency check, in one place: assertSameCurrency. Money throws a plain Error where the other files throw library exceptions. Code comments say this is on purpose, so these internal faults return a 500. It is not a bypass. The comment that mentions Order.assertSameCurrency describes a separate check at the aggregate boundary, and that file is outside this unit. The repeated non-empty-string checks are trivial field validation, not a duplicated domain rule. The addValidators() methods differ slightly: Money calls super and the others leave it empty. That is cosmetic and does not break the shared abstraction.

The unit has a single file, src/orders/infrastructure/repositories/order.repository.ts. Its only declaration is the OrderRepository class, an in-memory store for Order aggregates. All five methods (save, findById, findAll, delete, exists) work on the same private Map<string, Order>, so the file serves one persistence concern. The map key is always the order ID string, and save gets it through the aggregate's own accessor, order.id.getValue(), rather than reaching into the order's internals. No business rule or invariant is repeated here, since the repository only stores and retrieves Order objects. The application handlers inject the concrete class directly instead of going through a domain-level interface (port). That is a dependency-direction question, which this review excludes, so it does not affect the result.

This unit is one file, src/orders/presentation/orders.controller.ts, and it has one concern: exposing the order lifecycle over HTTP under the 'orders' route. Each handler only maps request parameters and bodies onto an application use-case input and hands it off. It holds no business rules or invariants, so none can be duplicated. Reads and writes take different paths: - Reads: getOrders and getOrder go through the QueryBus, using GetOrdersQuery and GetOrderQuery. - Writes: commands go through use-case services injected directly into the controller. This is a deliberate CQRS split that the controller applies the same way every time. It does not bypass the module's abstractions: no handler skips the application layer, and no handler talks to repositories or domain entities directly.

The unit has one empty barrel file (src/products/application/index.ts) and one saga file (src/products/application/sagas/product.saga.ts). ProductSaga uses the NestJS CQRS saga pattern throughout: three @Saga() members, each reacting to one product domain event (ProductCreatedEvent, ProductPriceChangedEvent, ProductStatusChangedEvent). The empty index.ts adds no other concern and duplicates nothing. Minor issues that are not failures: the delay(1000) and logging pattern is repeated, the code compares against the raw string 'INACTIVE' (a domain status type may exist but the source doesn't show one), and each saga returns `null as any` in place of a command. These are unfinished stubs, not a split concern or a copied invariant.

The four files cover one concern: the change-product-status use case. The service builds ChangeProductStatusCommand and sends it on the CommandBus. ChangeProductStatusCommandHandler loads the product, changes its status, checks broken rules, saves and commits. However, the set of valid statuses is defined twice within the unit. ChangeProductStatusDto hard-codes @IsIn(['ACTIVE', 'INACTIVE', 'DELETED']). The handler validates the same set again through ProductStatus.fromNameIgnoreCase and ProductStatus.getAll(). The two copies have already drifted: @IsIn is case-sensitive, while the handler ignores case. A value like 'inactive' is rejected by the DTO but would be accepted by the handler. The DTO comment says the copy is deliberate, so that a bad status returns a 400 naming the accepted values. That reason doesn't require a literal copy: the DTO could take its list from ProductStatus.getAll().map(s => s.name) and keep a single source of truth. The handler already turns an unknown name into an InvalidFormatException naming the accepted values. Minor point: ChangeProductStatusCommand's constructor takes the transport DTO instead of plain values, which ties the command to the HTTP contract. The concrete ProductRepository injection is an import-direction question and is out of scope.
violation_messages: ChangeProductStatusDto hard-codes @IsIn(['ACTIVE', 'INACTIVE', 'DELETED']), copying the closed set that ProductStatus already defines and that the command handler checks again with ProductStatus.fromNameIgnoreCase. The copies have drifted: the DTO is case-sensitive, the handler is not. Take the allowed values from ProductStatus.getAll() so the set is defined in one place.

rationale: All four files cover one concern, the create-product use case, and each file has a distinct role. CreateProductDto is the transport contract. It checks only structure, and its doc comment says domain invariants (Name 3–100 chars, positive Price) stay out of it on purpose, so no rule is duplicated. CreateProductCommand carries the DTO's fields onto the command bus. CreateProductService builds the command and dispatches it through CommandBus. CreateProductCommandHandler is the single place that assembles the aggregate. It builds the domain value objects (Name.create, Description.create, Price.create) and calls Product.create, then turns broken rules into a BrokenRulesException, persists the product and commits its events. No file skips the module's own flow (service → command → handler), and no invariant shows up in two places. The handler takes the concrete ProductRepository from infrastructure, but that is a layer-dependency question, which is out of scope here.

All four files handle a single concern, deleting a product. The service turns a call into a DeleteProductCommand and sends it through the CommandBus. The handler checks that the product exists, then deletes it. The command and DTO are plain data carriers for the same use case. The only invariant, that the product must exist before deletion, is enforced in one place: DeleteProductCommandHandler.execute. No file in the unit skips the module's own abstractions, because the service goes through the command/handler pipeline instead of calling the repository directly. One small inconsistency: DeleteProductDto declares `id`, but DeleteProductService.execute takes a raw `productId: string` and never uses the DTO. Whether that matters depends on how the controller uses it. It doesn't split the concerns or duplicate a rule, so it isn't a failure. The handler's dependency on infrastructure (ProductRepository) is an import-direction question, which is out of scope for this rule.

All four files serve one concern: updating a product. Each has its own role in a single CQRS flow. UpdateProductDto is the transport contract. UpdateProductService turns the DTO into an UpdateProductCommand and sends it on the CommandBus. UpdateProductCommand carries the data. UpdateProductCommandHandler loads the aggregate, applies changes through the entity's own methods and value-object factories, checks the aggregate's broken rules, saves, and publishes events. Each rule lives in one place. The DTO only checks transport types with class-validator. Domain rules stay in the value objects (Name.create, Description.create, Price.create) and the entity (isValid, brokenRules), and the handler does not repeat them. No file skips the module's own path: the service always goes through the command bus and never calls the handler or repository directly. The handler injects the concrete infrastructure ProductRepository, but that is a layer-dependency question and out of scope here. The truthy checks such as `if (price)` would skip a price of 0. That is a correctness concern, not a cohesion or duplication problem.

The five files have one concern: domain events for the Product aggregate. Every class extends AbstractDomainEvent from @nestjslatam/ddd-lib, passes EventMetadata to super, and rebuilds itself in a static fromJSON factory. Each fromJSON calls the shared helpers AbstractDomainEvent.extractMetadata and extractEventData, so no file bypasses the module's abstractions or re-implements metadata handling. The fromJSON factories have the same shape, but each one maps its own event's payload, so this is a per-event pattern rather than a shared rule copied into several places. There are two small inconsistencies, both cosmetic: (1) four constructors repeat assignments such as this.productId = productId even though the readonly parameter properties already set those fields, while ProductCreatedEvent does not; (2) the file ProductStatusChanged.ts exports ProductStatusChangedEvent, which breaks the *Event.ts file naming the other four files use. Neither one splits the module's concern, duplicates an invariant, or bypasses an abstraction, so the unit passes.

The structure is cohesive. All five classes extend AbstractRuleValidator<Product>, take the Product as their subject, and report problems through addBrokenRule. There is no split into unrelated concerns, and none of them bypass the module's abstraction. The problem is that some rules are not kept in one place: 1. **The rule that price can't be zero lives in two validators.** ProductPriceValidator.addRules already rejects any price <= 0. ProductStatusValidator.addRules checks for a zero price again ("Cannot activate product with zero price"). Since the price validator already blocks that case, the status check never fires on its own. The same rule now has two owners that can drift apart. 2. **Cross-field rules are split between two classes.** ProductBusinessRulesValidator exists for rules that compare fields (price vs. name length, description length vs. name length). The status/price rule is also a cross-field rule, but it sits in ProductStatusValidator, so there is no single home for these rules. 3. **Smaller consistency issues.** In ProductBusinessRulesValidator, the comment says "1000 veces" (1000 times) but the code uses `nameLength * 10000`. ProductNameValidator and ProductDescriptionValidator guard against a missing value, while ProductPriceValidator and ProductBusinessRulesValidator call `getValue()` directly with no guard. Point 1 is the clearest fail; points 2 and 3 support it. Overall, the unit fails the rule against duplicating an invariant or scattering it across files.
violation_messages: ProductStatusValidator.addRules checks for a zero price again ('Cannot activate product with zero price'), but ProductPriceValidator already rejects price <= 0. The same rule is in two places, and this check can never fire on its own. | ProductBusinessRulesValidator is meant to hold the cross-field rules, but the status/price cross-field rule lives in ProductStatusValidator, so these rules have no single home. The comment ('1000 veces') also contradicts the code (`nameLength * 10000`).

rationale: This module has a single file, product.repository.ts, and that file does one job: it stores Product aggregates in memory. The class ProductRepository has five methods (save, findById, findAll, delete, exists), and each one works on the same private Map<string, Product>. The file uses the domain's own identity abstraction: save keys entries by product.id.getValue() and does not build a key of its own. It doesn't repeat any domain rule or invariant, such as a validation check or a status-transition rule. There is no second file it could be split from or overlap with. The application command and query handlers inject the concrete class instead of an interface (a port). That is a dependency-direction question, which this rule leaves out of scope.

The module has one file, src/products/presentation/products.controller.ts. It holds a single class, ProductsController, which serves one concern: the HTTP routes for the products resource (create, list, get, update, change status, delete). Each handler only maps request parameters to an application call and returns the result. There is no business logic, validation rule or invariant written in the controller, so nothing is duplicated and nothing is split across concerns. Reads and writes go through different mechanisms. Reads use QueryBus with GetProductQuery and GetProductsQuery. Writes call injected use-case services directly. This is a common CQRS-lite style and does not bypass any abstraction. The write use cases are built as services (CreateProductService and the others, each with an execute method). The material shows no CommandBus, command classes or command handlers that the controller skips, so each application entry point is used the way it is built. The controller also never reaches past those entry points to repositories or domain entities.

This unit passes. All three files cover one concern: shared primitive value objects for the product domain. They use the module's abstractions the same way. Each class extends a value-object base from '@nestjslatam/ddd-lib' (StringValueObject or NumberValueObject), registers its rules through the addValidators() hook, and relies on a dedicated validator in './validators' (NameLengthValidator, DescriptionLengthValidator, PriceRangeValidator). Each domain rule lives in exactly one place, its validator. No file checks lengths or ranges inline, and none goes around the validator mechanism. The three static create() methods do repeat the same steps: build the object, check isValid, then throw BrokenRulesException with brokenRules.getBrokenRules(). This is a repeated construction pattern, not a duplicated domain rule. It could be moved into a shared generic factory or base helper, but that is a small maintainability point, not a broken boundary. The static load() methods intentionally skip validation so stored data can be rebuilt without re-checking it. They do this consistently across all three files. There is one small naming inconsistency: Name.ts is PascalCase, while description.ts and price.ts are lowercase. It does not affect cohesion.

The file holds only the IDomainReadRepository interface, with two method signatures: find() and findById(id). This is a persistence/data-access contract, which fits the declared infrastructure layer (path matches **/repositories/**). It contains no business rules, invariants, validation, domain behaviour, use-case orchestration or presentation logic. Under DDD convention, repository interfaces are sometimes placed in the domain layer as ports. Even so, nothing in the file carries a responsibility that belongs to another layer kind under this rubric.

This file passes. It is in the infrastructure layer (it matches **/repositories/**) and only declares IDomainWriteRepository, a generic contract for write operations: insert, insertBatch, update and delete. Persistence belongs to the infrastructure layer. The file has no business rules, no transport or presentation logic and no implementation code. In stricter DDD a repository interface is sometimes treated as a domain port. Even so, a pure persistence contract does not carry a responsibility from another layer, so it does not break the rubric. Which way the imports point (it imports the aggregate root) is checked by other tools and is not part of this review.

This file is a domain value object, and everything it does is domain work. It checks the identifier's own rules: the UUID format, null checks, lowercase normalisation, and the nil/empty identity. It defines equality and hashing based on the value. It provides factory methods (create/load/empty) and registers a validation rule that reads only the wrapped value. Nothing in it handles persistence, transport, HTTP, framework details or use-case orchestration. toJSON/toString just return the underlying value. That is a common value-object convenience, not infrastructure serialization. The comments mention an ORM, but only to explain why re-validation exists; no ORM code runs here. Using the uuid library for generation and validation is part of the value object's own invariant. Whether that dependency is allowed is an import-direction question, which is out of scope.

This file sits in the application layer, but it defines the HTTP request-body contract. Its own doc comment calls `CancelOrderBodyDto` "The transport contract for POST /orders/:id/cancel", and it uses class-validator `@IsString()` decorators to validate the incoming request body. That makes it presentation/transport work, which belongs to the infrastructure layer (presentation/controller). The application-level command shape `CancelOrderDto` is also built by extending this HTTP body class, so the use-case input inherits the transport contract and its validation. The comment says the controller merges in the path id, which ties the use-case input to how the HTTP route is laid out. On their own, DTO files with validation decorators are a common pattern and a borderline case. Here, though, the code states plainly that it is tied to a specific route, so the transport responsibility is misplaced.
violation_messages: CancelOrderBodyDto is described as 'The transport contract for POST /orders/:id/cancel' and uses class-validator `@IsString()` to validate the request body. That is presentation/transport work and belongs in the infrastructure (presentation) layer, not in an application use-case file. CancelOrderDto extends it, so the application command depends on the HTTP contract.

rationale: The file declares `CreateOrderDto`, a plain input shape. Its only extra content is structural and format checks from class-validator (`@IsString`, `@IsOptional`, `@IsEmail`). The layer model assigns `*.dto.ts` files to the application layer, and defining the input contract for a use case is that layer's role. The command and the service in the same use case consume this class. The file has no persistence, no HTTP handling, no routing and no framework wiring. It contains no business rules or domain invariants either. The doc comment calls the class a "transport contract" and mentions `ValidationPipe` and HTTP 400. That is a description, not logic: the code itself stays HTTP-agnostic. `@IsEmail` is a format check on input, not a business rule. One point is debatable. Some teams would keep transport-specific validation in a presentation-layer request DTO and give the application layer an undecorated one. This file carries no behaviour that would make that separation required, so I did not count it as a violation.

DeliverOrderCommandHandler.execute only does use-case orchestration, which is the application layer's role. It loads the aggregate through the repository, delegates the state change to the domain (order.deliver()), checks the validity result the domain reports (order.isValid / brokenRules), saves through the repository, and publishes domain events through EventPublisher. The file has no persistence code (no queries or ORM mapping), no transport code (no request or response handling) and no business rules of its own. Using NestJS's HTTP-flavoured NotFoundException leaks a little transport meaning, but it only signals that the order wasn't found and adds no transport responsibility. The import of the infrastructure OrderRepository is an import-direction question, which is out of scope.

The file only defines DeliverOrderCommand, an immutable application-layer command object. Its constructor copies orderId from DeliverOrderDto. Mapping a DTO to a command is an application-layer job. The file has no persistence, transport or framework logic, and no business rules that belong in the domain layer.

The file has only immutable domain event classes. Each one is a constructor with readonly properties that carry domain data: IDs, amounts, statuses and timestamps. It has no persistence, transport, framework decorators, serialization or orchestration logic. It also has no business rules that belong in another layer. Domain events modelling things that happened in the Order aggregate are a domain-layer job. The import from @nestjslatam/ddd-lib is only used for the IdValueObject type. Import direction is out of scope for this rule.

The file sits in the domain layer and only holds domain invariant validation for the Order aggregate's customer info. It checks that customer info, email and name are present, that email and phone have a valid format, and that the name has a minimum length. It has no persistence, transport, HTTP or framework orchestration logic. AbstractRuleValidator comes from a DDD support library (@nestjslatam/ddd-lib) for domain rule validation, not from a framework transport or persistence layer. Import direction is out of scope.

This file is a domain validator, and everything it does fits the domain layer. OrderItemProductValidator.addRules() checks the OrderItem's own state against business invariants: the product ID must be present, and the product name must be present and between 3 and 500 characters. It records failures with addBrokenRule. The file has no persistence, transport, HTTP, database or other framework logic. It does extend AbstractRuleValidator from @nestjslatam/ddd-lib, but that library provides DDD building blocks for domain modelling, not infrastructure. Whether that import is allowed is an import-direction question, which is out of scope here.

The file sits in the infrastructure layer. Everything it does is persistence: an in-memory Map-backed repository for Order aggregates with save, findById, findAll, delete and exists. It contains no business rules, no domain invariants and no use-case orchestration. The @Injectable decorator is NestJS framework wiring, which belongs in infrastructure. Using order.id.getValue() as the storage key is a mechanical step for persistence, not business logic.

OrdersController sits in the infrastructure layer, and everything in it is transport work. The NestJS route decorators map HTTP routes. Params, query strings and bodies are pulled out of the request and turned into use-case input objects or CQRS queries, and the work is handed to application services or the QueryBus. The file sets HTTP status codes and shapes the response, as in `createOrder` returning `{ id }`. It contains no business rules: no order state-transition checks, no quantity validation and no pricing. It also contains no persistence logic. That role fits an infrastructure/presentation adapter.

This file is in the application layer. It holds an event handler that reacts to a domain event, ProductCreatedEvent, and only logs it. Reacting to domain events is normal application-layer work. The handler has no persistence, transport or business rules, so nothing in it belongs to another layer. It uses NestJS CQRS decorators and Logger, but that is a framework hook used to wire up the handler, not infrastructure logic. Some comments list possible future work, such as caching and external integrations, but they are not code.

The orchestration in execute() is a proper application-layer job: it checks that the product exists, then calls the repository to delete it. The @CommandHandler decorator is ordinary NestJS CQRS wiring for a use case, so I accept it here. The problem is the failure path. When the product is missing, the handler throws NotFoundException from @nestjs/common. That is an HTTP exception that maps to a 404 response, so the use case is deciding the transport-level result itself. That decision belongs to the presentation/infrastructure layer, for example a controller or an exception filter that turns an application error into an HTTP status. The use case should instead throw an application or domain error such as ProductNotFoundError. The import of the infrastructure ProductRepository is an import-direction issue, so it is out of scope and not judged. My confidence is moderate because many NestJS codebases accept this pattern.
violation_messages: DeleteProductCommandHandler.execute() throws NestJS's HTTP NotFoundException (404). Choosing the HTTP status is a transport job that belongs to the presentation/infrastructure layer, such as a controller or exception filter. The use case should throw an application or domain error, such as ProductNotFoundError, and let the presentation layer turn it into a 404.

rationale: The file holds one plain command object, DeleteProductCommand, with a single readonly productId field that is set in the constructor. A command message like this is a normal application-layer responsibility in CQRS and use-case designs. The file has no persistence, transport, framework or HTTP logic, and it has no domain business rules. Everything in it belongs to the application layer.

The file defines a domain event, ProductStatusChangedEvent, that carries productId and productStatus. This is a normal domain-layer job: it records a business fact that happened on the Product aggregate. The static fromJSON factory rebuilds the event from a plain record using helpers from the base class (extractMetadata and extractEventData). It does no I/O and does not touch any transport or persistence framework. It is a small rebuild factory, which is common for domain events in DDD libraries, so it does not count as infrastructure logic. The file contains no business rules that belong elsewhere and no repository, HTTP or database code.

The file sits in the domain layer and holds only domain business-rule validation for the Product aggregate. ProductBusinessRulesValidator.addRules() reads the aggregate's value objects (name, price, description) and records broken rules through addBrokenRule. It does no persistence, transport, HTTP or framework work, and it has no application orchestration. The base class AbstractRuleValidator comes from a DDD library, which is a domain-modeling helper and not infrastructure. Import direction is out of scope for this rule.

The file is a domain validator for the Product aggregate. Its only job is checking domain invariants: status must be present, status must be a valid ProductStatus value, and an ACTIVE product cannot have a zero price. These are business rules, so they belong in the domain layer. The file has no persistence, transport, HTTP or framework orchestration logic. It extends AbstractRuleValidator from a DDD support library, which is a domain-modeling base class and not infrastructure. Whether that import is allowed is an import-direction question, which is out of scope here.

The file sits in the infrastructure layer, and everything it does is persistence work, which is the job of that layer. ProductRepository keeps Product aggregates in an in-memory Map and has only storage methods: save, findById, findAll, delete and exists. It has no business rules, no validation, no orchestration that would belong in the application layer, and no transport or presentation logic. Using the NestJS @Injectable decorator is framework wiring, which is also fine in infrastructure. The application handlers inject the concrete repository rather than a port, but that is a dependency-direction concern and out of scope for this rule.

ProductsController sits in the infrastructure layer (presentation/transport). It only does transport-adapter work: it declares HTTP routes and status codes with NestJS decorators, pulls path, query and body parameters, builds query objects, and hands the work to application services or the QueryBus. It holds no business rules (no validation logic, no status-transition checks, no computations) and does no persistence. Wrapping the created id as { id } is response shaping, which is normal transport work. All of its responsibilities fit an infrastructure/presentation adapter.

This unit passes. The src/infrastructure module is the infrastructure composition root, and its six files share one concern: cross-cutting technical adapters. They cover the idempotency decorator and interceptor, the domain event publisher adapter, logging, tracing bootstrap, and the global Nest module that wires these together. Each piece goes through the module's own abstractions: - IdempotencyInterceptor depends on the IdempotencyStore port, not on Redis directly. - The @Idempotent decorator is a thin wrapper around that interceptor, so the idempotency logic lives in one place. - EventEmitter2DomainEventPublisher implements the DomainEventPublisher port and is bound to it in InfrastructureModule. - WinstonLoggerService reads its settings through EnvConfigService and gets correlation IDs from CorrelationService. - Middleware order is defined once, in InfrastructureModule.configure. There are some small inconsistencies, but none rises to a rubric failure: - tracing.ts reads process.env (NODE_ENV, OTEL_*) directly instead of using EnvConfigService. This is defensible because the OTel SDK has to start before Nest bootstraps. - The interceptor uses the Redis-specific constant IDEMPOTENCY_REDIS.RETRY_AFTER_SECONDS. - The winston file shows the same DailyRotateFile settings several times. That is repetition inside one file, not a rule or invariant spread across files. I found no unrelated concerns, no duplicated invariant across files, and no clear bypass of the module's abstractions.

Both files handle one concern: RS256 JWT key material and verification. jwks.service.ts derives the public CryptoKey, kid and JWKS from the configured private key and implements JwksPort. jwt-verifier.service.ts uses that key only through the JwksPort abstraction (constructor-injected, getPublicKey()), not by reaching into JwksService internals. Each file owns its own rules. Key handling (RS256, kid thumbprint, private-field stripping) lives only in jwks.service.ts. Verification policy (VERIFY_OPTIONS issuer/clockTolerance, token-type checks, payload narrowing) lives only in jwt-verifier.service.ts. Neither file repeats a rule from the other. The three private assert helpers repeat the shared checks on sub/iss/iat/exp, but that is minor repetition inside one class, not a split invariant or a bypassed abstraction.

All five files cover one concern: they are input shapes for analytics read queries. They contain only type declarations, with no logic, so no rule or invariant is repeated in executable code. TopProductsQuery and PaymentsTimeSeriesQuery both extend the shared AnalyticsPeriodQuery. PaymentsTimeSeriesQuery takes its AnalyticsBucket type from analytics.policy, so it doesn't redefine bucket values locally. One small inconsistency: AnalyticsOverviewQuery declares its own from/to fields instead of extending AnalyticsPeriodQuery. That repeats two fields, not a business rule, and it may be intentional because the overview query also carries the comparison window that the use case computes. It is worth tidying up, but it is not enough to fail the unit.

The unit is one cohesive concern: HTTP query and response DTOs plus one validator for the analytics controller. Most files use the module's policy constants consistently. AnalyticsPeriodQueryDto is the shared base for the period queries. ANALYTICS_MAX_RANGE_DAYS is read from analytics.policy by both the validator and the query DTO. The attention statuses come from ATTENTION_ORDER_STATUSES. PaymentsTimeSeriesQueryDto takes the bucket whitelist from ANALYTICS_BUCKETS / AnalyticsBucket. However, PaymentsTimeSeriesResponseDto skips that abstraction: it hard-codes the bucket list as the literal type 'day' | 'week' and enum ['day', 'week']. The same invariant (the allowed bucket sizes) is therefore defined in two places. If the policy changes, the query and response contracts will drift apart. The hard-coded 'UTC' timezone literal is repeated in three response DTOs, which is a smaller instance of the same pattern.
violation_messages: PaymentsTimeSeriesResponseDto.bucket hard-codes `enum: ['day', 'week']` and the type `'day' | 'week'` instead of using ANALYTICS_BUCKETS / AnalyticsBucket from analytics.policy. PaymentsTimeSeriesQueryDto uses those policy constants, so the bucket whitelist is now defined in two places and the two contracts can drift apart.

rationale: This module only declares the authentication module's outbound ports, and all three files serve that one concern. identity.gateway.ts (IdentityGateway, UserRecord, CreateUserInput) covers user identity. authorization.gateway.ts (AuthorizationGateway, RoleRecord) covers role assignment and lookup. jwt-signer.port.ts (JwtSignerPort and its payload and result types) covers token signing. No file repeats a rule or invariant from another: UserRecord and RoleRecord do not overlap, and the mustChangePassword claim rule is documented only in SignAccessTokenPayload. The use cases inject all three ports, and adapters and mocks implement them, so nothing bypasses the abstractions. There are three small inconsistencies. JwtSignerPort returns plain Promise<string> while the gateways return Result<..., InfrastructureError>. signCartSessionToken brings a cart concern into the auth signer, but it is still token signing. File suffixes mix .gateway.ts and .port.ts. None of these splits the module into unrelated concerns or duplicates a rule, so the unit passes.

Both files serve the same concern (seeding auth users), but each one carries its own full copy of the user-provisioning saga, so the same rollback rule lives in two places. The steps are: find the user by email, hash the password, create the identity, save the credential with mustChangePassword true, assign the role, and roll back in reverse order on failure. The copies have already drifted. The super-admin use case checks for a minimum password length of 6; the demo seeder doesn't. The demo seeder resets the credentials of existing users; the super-admin use case doesn't. Only the demo seeder passes phone to createUser. The result types differ too: only SeededDemoAuthUser includes userId. SeedDemoAuthUsersUseCase also seeds a super admin itself instead of reusing SeedSuperAdminUseCase, so the module has two independent ways to create a super admin.
violation_messages: SeedSuperAdminUseCase.execute repeats the user-provisioning saga from SeedDemoAuthUsersUseCase.seedUser: create identity, save credential with mustChangePassword, assign role, and roll back in reverse order. It also checks password length inline (< 6), a rule the other seeding path doesn't apply. | SeedDemoAuthUsersUseCase.seedUser has its own copy of the provisioning and rollback flow, and seeds a SUPER_ADMIN itself instead of sharing code with SeedSuperAdminUseCase. The copies already differ: it resets existing users, passes phone, and skips the password check.

rationale: All seven files serve one concern: the HTTP request and response contracts for the authentication controller. They use the same abstractions throughout (@nestjs/swagger ApiProperty plus class-validator decorators), and nothing bypasses the module's abstractions. The one problem is the password-length rule. "At least 6 characters" is hardcoded as a literal in two separate DTOs, and in each one it is written twice: once in the class-validator `@MinLength(6)` and once in the Swagger `minLength: 6`. ChangePasswordDto.newPassword and RegisterDto.password should enforce the same password policy, but nothing shares it, such as a constant or a composed decorator. If someone changes it in one place, registration and password change can silently end up with different rules, and the API docs can disagree with the actual validation. Other repetition is acceptable as boundary-contract duplication: the email `@IsEmail()` checks and the phone/name fields that appear in both RegisterDto and RegisterResponseDto. Repeated decorators are common in DTOs, which is why confidence is moderate.
violation_messages: ChangePasswordDto.newPassword hardcodes the password minimum length (@MinLength(6) and Swagger minLength: 6). The same rule is repeated in RegisterDto.password, so the password policy is not defined in one place. | RegisterDto.password repeats the hardcoded password minimum length (@MinLength(6) and Swagger minLength: 6) that is also in ChangePasswordDto.newPassword. Move it to a shared constant or decorator.

rationale: Both unit files are thin HTTP adapters for one concern: managing roles and permissions in the authorization module. They follow the same pattern. Each class is protected by the module's own `RequirePermissions` decorator, injects application use cases from `core/application/usecases`, documents responses with DTOs from `primary-adapter/dto`, and returns the use case result without adding business logic in the controller. Neither file goes around the module's abstractions, for example by accessing repositories or the ORM directly. No rule or invariant is duplicated. The class-level `@RequirePermissions('manage_roles')` on each controller is the usual way to declare access per route group. The method-level override on `RolesController.findAll` (`'manage_roles', 'view_all_users'`) is a deliberate refinement of that rule, not a copy of it. The controllers sit at the module root rather than under `primary-adapter/`, which is a minor placement inconsistency, but it does not break cohesion or how the abstractions are used.

The four files all handle persistence for the authorization module's domain repository ports, and they follow the same conventions: - Each class implements a domain port (`RoleRepository`, `PermissionRepository`, `UserRoleAssignmentRepository`). - Each returns `Result<T, RepositoryError>` and wraps failures with `ErrorFactory.RepositoryError`. - Each converts between ORM and domain objects through its own mapper (`RoleMapper`, `PermissionMapper`, `UserRoleAssignmentMapper`). `CachedRoleRepository` wraps any `RoleRepository` and delegates all persistence to it, so it never touches the ORM directly. It adds caching only around permission codes. The cache-key rule (`rolePermissionsCacheKey`) and the invalidation logic (`invalidatePermissionCache`) each live in one place. The rule for syncing the role-permission join table lives only in `PostgresRoleRepository.syncRolePermissions`. That method reads `PermissionEntity` through the transaction's entity manager. This is a reasonable choice for transactional consistency inside the same persistence adapter, not a bypass. Minor inconsistencies are style, not cohesion problems: - `postgres-user-role-assignment.repository.ts` uses absolute `src/` imports where the others use relative paths. - In that same file, the `UserRoleAssignmentEntity` repository field is named `roleRepo`. - `findAll` uses `entities.map(RoleMapper.toDomain)` where the permission repository uses `PermissionMapper.toDomainArray`.

The unit has one file, src/modules/carts/carts.controller.ts, and it covers a single concern: the HTTP surface for cart management. Each endpoint is a thin adapter. It reads the route params, body DTO and CallerContext, then passes them to the matching application use case. The controller holds no business rules, such as quantity checks, ownership checks or cart creation logic, so no invariant is duplicated here that should live in the use cases or the domain. It uses the module's own abstractions consistently. Every handler goes through an injected use case, and none reaches into a repository or ORM directly. Every handler receives the caller through @CallerCtx(). Authorization is declared once, at class level, with @RequirePermissions('manage_own_cart'), not repeated on each method. One small inconsistency: the controller sits at the module root instead of under the module's primary-adapters/ folder, where its DTOs live. That is a matter of where the file is placed, not a split in concerns or a bypass of the module's abstractions, so it does not fail the rubric.

All three files support the carts application layer and fit together. `cart-presentation.result.ts` defines the read-model contract (`CartPresentationDTO`, `CartItemPresentationDTO`). `cart-presentation.mapper.ts` builds that contract from the `Cart` domain entity and uses the entity's own values (`totalAmount`, `itemCount`, `item.subtotal`) instead of recalculating them. `cart-ownership.validator.ts` holds the cart access/ownership rule in one injectable class, which four use cases inject (AddCartItem, ClearCart, RemoveCartItem, UpdateCartItem), so the rule lives in one place. None of the files duplicates a rule or invariant held by another file in the unit. None bypasses the module's abstractions: the validator uses the shared-kernel `Result`, `ErrorFactory` and `CallerContext`/`isSystemCaller` the way the rest of the module does. There are two minor concerns, and neither fails the rubric on the material provided: 1. `CartPresentationMapper.fromDomain` hardcodes `shippingCost = 0` and calculates `totalAmount` as subtotal + shippingCost. That is a small pricing rule inside a mapper. 2. `secondary-adapters/mappers/query/cart-query.mapper.ts` also uses the presentation DTO and may repeat this calculation, but that file is not part of this unit and could not be checked.

All four use cases share one concern: changing a user's addresses through the User aggregate. Each one loads with userRepository.findByIdForUpdate, calls an aggregate method, then calls save. That part is consistent. However, two rules are copied into all four use cases, and the copies differ. (1) Each file repeats the rule that a failed ownership check is reported as 'not found'. Only the add use case passes HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND; the other three use the ErrorFactory default. Callers therefore get different HTTP behaviour for the same failure. (2) The same is true of the 'user not found' handling after loading the user. The message also differs: 'User not found' in add and delete, versus `User with id ${userId} not found` in set-default and update. In addition, the input types are defined two ways. Add and update take command classes from application/commands. Delete and set-default each declare their own input interface inside the use-case file. The code also checks for failure two ways: isFailure(userResult) in some places and userResult.isFailure in others. Because these checks are copied instead of kept in one place, the unit fails the rubric.
violation_messages: The 'not found' handling for a failed ownership check and a missing user is copied here, and it differs from the other use cases: this file passes HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND explicitly and the others don't. This rule should live in one shared place. | This file declares its own DeleteAddressInput instead of using the command classes that the sibling use cases use. It also repeats the ownership and missing-user checks without the NOT_FOUND status and with the message 'User not found'. | This file declares its own SetDefaultAddressInput instead of using a command class. It also repeats the ownership and missing-user checks, and its handling differs from the add use case. | This file repeats the ownership and missing-user checks but leaves out the HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND that the add use case passes.

rationale: Both files define abstract repository classes for entities in the identity domain, so the unit serves one concern. `AddressRepository` is the port for `Address` and `UserRepository` is the port for `User`. Both use the same shared-kernel types: every method returns `Promise<Result<..., RepositoryError>>`. Neither file holds business rules or invariants, so nothing is duplicated, and neither bypasses the module's abstractions. There are some style inconsistencies, but none of them breaks the rule: - **Import paths:** `address.repository.ts` imports `src/shared-kernel/...` by absolute path, while `user.repository.ts` uses relative paths. - **Write methods:** `AddressRepository` has separate `create` and `update` methods. `UserRepository` has a single `save` with optimistic concurrency through `expectedVersion` and `findByIdForUpdate`. - **Empty results:** `AddressRepository.findByUserId` returns `Address[] | null`, while `UserRepository.findAll` returns `User[]`. One open question: the graph shows address use cases (`AddAddressUseCase`, `DeleteAddressUseCase`) injecting `UserRepository`. That could mean `Address` belongs to the `User` aggregate and that `AddressRepository` overlaps with it. The material I was given doesn't show whether those use cases also inject `AddressRepository`, or how `User` stores addresses. I can't confirm a duplicated persistence path from that alone.

All seven files serve one concern: the HTTP request and response DTOs for the identity module (users and addresses). The unit still fails because two rules are written out in more than one place. (1) The role-code format regex /^[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*$/ is copied into AssignRoleDto and ListUsersQueryDto, and the two copies already have different error messages. (2) UpdateAddressDto repeats every field and validator from AddAddressDto, only adding @IsOptional to each, instead of being derived from it. If either rule changes, several files must be edited by hand. Smaller consistency issues: update-address.dto.ts imports AddressType with an 'src/...' path while the other address DTOs use a relative path, and AddressResponseDto types its timestamps as Date while the user response DTOs use ISO strings.
violation_messages: The role-code format regex /^[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*$/ on AssignRoleDto.roleCode is also in ListUsersQueryDto, with a different message. It should be defined once and reused. | ListUsersQueryDto.roleCode repeats the role-code regex from AssignRoleDto instead of using a shared definition. | UpdateAddressDto repeats every address field and validator from AddAddressDto instead of being derived from it (e.g. PartialType/OmitType). It also imports AddressType with an 'src/...' path, unlike the other address DTOs.

rationale: The unit has a single file, src/modules/inventory/inventory.controller.ts, and it handles one concern: exposing inventory operations over HTTP. Every handler is a thin delegate that passes request data to the matching injected use case (GetInventoryUseCase, ListInventoryUseCase, AdjustStockUseCase, ReserveStockUseCase, ReleaseStockUseCase, CheckStockUseCase, ListLowStockUseCase, BulkCheckStockUseCase). The only mapping happens in adjustStock and checkStock, which combine the productId path parameter with body or query data. The controller does not reach past the use cases into repositories or domain entities, and it contains no business logic. Two domain rules are only described in Swagger text, not implemented here: missing inventory counts as unavailable, and the low-stock threshold. Those rules presumably live in the use cases. The controller uses the module's request and response DTOs from primary-adapters/dto consistently. Repeating the permission strings in @RequirePermissions is ordinary declarative metadata, not a duplicated invariant. Import direction and layer placement are out of scope.

The three files cover a single concern: the data shapes of the Order aggregate, meaning the order, its line items and its shipping address. order.interface.ts builds IOrder and IOrderEditable from IOrderItem and the shipping-address interfaces instead of redefining their fields. Address fields are declared only once, in IShippingAddressEditable, and IShippingAddress extends it with an id. IOrderEditable follows the same pattern by reusing IShippingAddressEditable. No rule or invariant is repeated: the totals fields (lineTotal, subtotal, totalPrice) are only declared, and no file computes them. No file goes around the module's own abstractions. Two small points don't change the result. IOrderItem has no 'Editable' variant, unlike the order and address interfaces. And the header comment in order.interface.ts gives an old path (src/modules/orders/domain/interfaces/...) instead of the real location under core/domain. Import paths are out of scope.

The unit is a single file that declares one interface, RawOrderListQueryRow. It describes the raw row shape that the TypeORM query builder returns for order list projections. That is one concern. The file holds no logic and no invariants, so no rule can be duplicated across files. Nothing in it goes around the module's own abstractions. The only consumers are the query adapter, the query mapper and a testing factory, all of which work with raw persistence rows. That matches the interface's stated purpose. Its placement under the secondary-adapters folder is a layer question, which is out of scope here.

All eight files cover one concern: the request and response DTOs for the payments HTTP endpoints. That part is fine. The problem is how they use the module's types and where they put their rules. 1. **Status and payment-method types are inconsistent.** `PaymentResponseDto` types `status` as `PaymentStatusType` and `paymentMethod` as `PaymentMethodType`. `CreatePaymentDto` validates `paymentMethod` with `@IsEnum(PaymentMethodType)`. But `PaymentDetailResponseDto`, `PaymentListItemResponseDto` and `ListPaymentsQueryDto` use plain `string` for status and payment method. The query filter `status` has no enum validation at all. So those three files skip the enum types their sibling files use. 2. **The payment read model is defined three times.** `PaymentResponseDto`, `PaymentDetailResponseDto` and `PaymentListItemResponseDto` repeat mostly the same fields (id, orderId, userId, amount, currency, status, paymentMethod, transactionId, createdAt) without sharing a base. The copies have already drifted: - dates are `Date` in one and `string` in the others; - `userId` and `transactionId` are optional in one and required in the others; - `gatewayPaymentIntentId` is optional in one and required-but-nullable in another. 3. **The positive-amount rule is repeated with different values.** `CreatePaymentDto.amount` uses `@Min(0)`, which lets a zero payment through. `ProcessRefundDto.amount` and `RecordCodPaymentDto.amountCollected` use `@Min(0.01)`. 4. **Pagination limits are documented but not enforced.** `ListPaymentsQueryDto` declares a minimum and maximum for `page` and `limit` only in the Swagger `@ApiPropertyOptional` metadata. There are no `@Min`/`@Max` validators, so the API docs describe a rule that is never checked. Confidence is moderate because some of the divergence could be on purpose, for example different minimums for payments and refunds.
violation_messages: `status` and `paymentMethod` are plain `string`, not the module's `PaymentStatusType`/`PaymentMethodType` used in `PaymentResponseDto`. It also repeats the payment read-model fields of `PaymentListItemResponseDto` and `PaymentResponseDto`, with different date types (string vs Date) and different optional/required fields. | `PaymentListItemResponseDto` repeats the payment read-model fields of `PaymentDetailResponseDto` instead of sharing them, and types `status`/`paymentMethod` as `string` instead of the module enums. | The `status` filter is an unvalidated `string`, not `PaymentStatusType`. The page/limit bounds (min 1, max 100) appear only in Swagger metadata, with no `@Min`/`@Max` validators to enforce them. | `amount` uses `@Min(0)`, while `ProcessRefundDto` and `RecordCodPaymentDto` use `@Min(0.01)`. The positive-amount rule is repeated with values that disagree.

rationale: Both files do one job: they define the TypeORM persistence schema for the payments aggregate. PaymentEntity maps the 'payments' table and RefundEntity maps the 'refunds' table. They are linked by a matching two-way relationship: PaymentEntity.refunds uses OneToMany, and RefundEntity.payment uses ManyToOne with JoinColumn 'payment_id'. Both files follow the same conventions: snake_case column names, the same decimal(10,2) setting for money, varchar(3) for currency, and the same created_at and updated_at date columns. Neither file holds business logic or an invariant that is repeated elsewhere. One small inconsistency: RefundEntity.status is typed as plain string, while PaymentEntity.status uses the domain type PaymentStatusType. No refund-status type appears in the provided material, so this is not clearly a bypass of an existing abstraction, and it is not enough to fail the unit.

All eight files share one job: they are the HTTP request and response contracts for the products module's primary adapters, covering products and categories. Every file uses the same tools in the same way: class-validator for input validation, class-transformer for converting query-string values, and @nestjs/swagger for API docs. The update DTOs reuse the create DTOs through PartialType instead of redefining fields. ProductDetailResponseDto extends ProductListItemResponseDto, so the list fields are defined once. PaginatedProductsResponseDto builds on the list item DTO. No file reaches around these shared pieces with ad-hoc validation or parsing. There is one small repeat: the same `isActive` query-string-to-boolean conversion appears in both list-query DTOs. It is a two-line piece of input parsing, not a business rule, so it is not enough to fail the module. Products and categories belong to the same bounded module, as the folder structure shows, so having DTOs for both is not a split into unrelated concerns.

The file only holds configuration for retrying background jobs: a BackoffStrategy enum, a RetryConfig interface and a DEFAULT_RETRY_CONFIG constant. Retry, backoff and job settings are technical concerns, and they belong in the infrastructure layer. The file has no business rules, no domain invariants and no presentation logic. Only infrastructure job files import it (job-config.service.ts, job-retry-policies.ts and retry-strategy.ts), which fits its role as infrastructure configuration.

The file sits in src/infrastructure and its job is technical cache maintenance for Redis. It reacts to Redis reconnect events, bumps the cache generation, drops RediSearch indexes from the previous generation, clears the cache-aside 'is cached' flags, sets the indexes up again, and records a metric and a log entry when recovery fails. All of this is persistence and caching infrastructure. It contains no business or domain rules and no transport or presentation logic. The '.service.ts' suffix could also match the application file pattern, but the file is under src/infrastructure/** and its responsibilities belong to infrastructure.

The rule passes. ShutdownService belongs to the infrastructure layer, and everything it does is infrastructure work. It hooks into the NestJS lifecycle (BeforeApplicationShutdown and OnApplicationShutdown). It starts a safety timer that forces the process to exit if shutdown stalls, and it uses unref so that timer doesn't keep the process alive. It also logs and tracks whether shutdown has started. It implements a domain-defined port (ApplicationLifecyclePort), which is the normal pattern for an infrastructure adapter. The file contains no business rules, domain invariants or use-case orchestration. The *.service.ts filename matches an application-layer pattern, but the declared layer is infrastructure and the work done fits that layer.

The file is declared as domain because its path matches **/core/**. Its path also matches application patterns (**/application/**, **/queries/**). It contains only three plain TypeScript interfaces describing a read-model result shape: AnalyticsKpiSnapshot, OrderAttentionCount and AnalyticsOverviewResult. There is no persistence logic (no SQL, ORM or repository calls), no transport or framework logic (no HTTP, decorators or serialization), and no behaviour of any kind. Conceptually it is an application-level query result DTO, so it fits the application layer better than the domain layer. That mismatch comes from how the path patterns overlap, not from a responsibility the file carries. The rubric's failure cases are persistence, transport or framework logic in a domain file, or business rules in infrastructure or presentation, and none of them apply. The comment "Persisted order status string" only documents what the field contains; the file does no persistence work. No ADR prose was given that would contradict this.

The unit is declared as domain because its path matches **/core/**. Its main job is application orchestration, not domain modelling. RegisterUserUseCase.execute coordinates outbound ports (IdentityGateway, AuthorizationGateway, CredentialRepository, PasswordHasher) and runs a multi-step workflow with manual compensating rollbacks (saga-style). That is use-case or application-layer work. The file also carries transport concerns: it maps failures to HTTP status codes with HttpStatus from @nestjs/common (INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, CONFLICT). It also depends on framework DI through the @Injectable() decorator. HTTP status mapping and framework wiring do not belong in a domain file. The HTTP status codes would also be misplaced if the file were classified under its likely intended application layer. The layer classification itself looks like a misconfiguration, since the path also matches **/application/** and **/usecases/** and the name matches *.usecase.ts. Even so, the file's responsibilities do not match its declared domain role.
violation_messages: RegisterUserUseCase.execute maps failures to HTTP status codes (HttpStatus.CONFLICT, HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR from @nestjs/common). That is a transport/presentation (infrastructure) concern inside a file declared as domain. | The @Injectable() decorator puts NestJS framework DI concerns, which belong to infrastructure, into a domain-layer unit. | RegisterUserUseCase.execute coordinates gateways and repositories with compensating rollbacks (identityGateway.deleteUser, credentialRepository.deleteByUserId). This is application-layer use-case orchestration, not a domain responsibility.

rationale: ChangePasswordDto is a plain input contract for the change-password use case. Its only job is to declare the shape of the request (currentPassword, newPassword) and to validate input syntax (IsString, MinLength). That is the usual role of an application-layer DTO. The @ApiProperty decorators add transport documentation metadata, but they are declarative annotations on the same input contract. They contain no HTTP handling, routing, persistence or domain logic. The file is also located under primary-adapters and is used by the controller, so it serves as the inbound adapter's input contract. That is consistent with how DTOs are classified here. No business rules, persistence or framework orchestration logic is misplaced in the file.

RegisterResponseDto describes the shape of the register response (id, firstName, lastName, email, phone, isActive) and has no behaviour. That fits an application-layer DTO, whose job is to shape data crossing a boundary. There is no persistence, no request handling or HTTP status logic, and no business rules. The one concern is the @ApiProperty and @ApiPropertyOptional decorators from @nestjs/swagger. They document the HTTP API, which is a transport concern, and the file sits under primary-adapters/, which suggests the project treats it as an adapter; it was assigned to the application layer only because it matches **/dto/** and *.dto.ts. The decorators are declarative labels, not running code, and the rubric's failure examples are about misplaced logic, so I treat them as a minor coupling to the web framework rather than a misplaced responsibility. Hence a pass with moderate confidence.

This file is a TypeORM persistence schema in the infrastructure layer. It only maps a table: it sets column types, precision and scale, a numeric transformer, a default value and the relationship to CartEntity with cascade delete. All of that is persistence-mapping work, which belongs in infrastructure. The file has no business rules, validation, pricing logic, transport code or presentation code. The column default 'USD' is a storage-level default, not a domain rule.

src/modules/identity/core/application/commands/create-user.command.ts only declares the CreateUserCommand interface, a plain data shape with primitive fields (firstName, lastName, email, optional phone). It has no functions, methods or other statements carrying behaviour, so it contains no persistence, transport, framework logic or business rules. The file is labelled domain only because its path contains 'core/' (matched by the domain glob **/core/**). Its path segments 'application/commands/' and its *.command.ts name also match the application layer's patterns, so the layer label is ambiguous. Conceptually, a command message is a use-case input contract, which is arguably an application concern. But a pure data type with no behaviour carries no responsibility the domain layer cannot hold, so it is not counted as misplaced. The ambiguity is in the layer model, not in this file's code. Confidence is moderate: a stricter reading that treats any use-case input contract as application-only would fail the file.

This file is declared as domain because its path contains `/core/`. It is really an application use case, as its `/application/usecases/` path and `.usecase.ts` suffix show. `SetDefaultAddressUseCase.execute` coordinates a full transaction. It runs an access-policy check, loads the aggregate through `userRepository.findByIdForUpdate`, delegates to `user.setDefaultAddress`, and saves through `userRepository.save(user, expectedVersion)` with an optimistic-concurrency version. That is application-layer coordination, not domain behaviour. The class also carries the NestJS `@Injectable()` decorator, which is framework dependency-injection wiring. A domain file should not hold either responsibility. The business rule itself stays in the entity (`user.setDefaultAddress`), so there is no misplaced business logic. The problem is that the file's responsibilities match the application layer, not the declared domain layer. The mismatch probably comes from the layer patterns overlapping, but under the given model it still breaks the rule.
violation_messages: This file is declared as domain, but `SetDefaultAddressUseCase.execute` does application-layer work. It checks caller access with `OwnedResourceAccessPolicy`, loads the user with `userRepository.findByIdForUpdate`, and saves with `userRepository.save(user, expectedVersion)`. The class is also marked with the NestJS `@Injectable()` decorator, which is framework wiring. Both responsibilities belong to the application layer, not domain.

rationale: The file is assigned to the application layer only because its path matches **/dto/**. What it actually does is define an HTTP query-string contract for inventory.controller.ts, which is an infrastructure file. Three things make it a transport concern. First, `@ApiPropertyOptional` from @nestjs/swagger adds OpenAPI documentation (example, minimum, description), which is HTTP transport documentation. Second, `@Type(() => Number)` from class-transformer turns the raw query-string value into a number, which is request-parsing logic. Third, the class models query parameters for a specific HTTP endpoint, and the folder name `primary-adapters` says the same thing. All of this belongs to the infrastructure (primary/driving adapter) layer, not to a framework-independent application input contract. This is a borderline case: validation DTOs often sit in the application layer. But Swagger annotations and query-string coercion are transport responsibilities, so the file's job does not match its declared layer.
violation_messages: CheckStockQueryDto is an HTTP transport contract: Swagger `@ApiPropertyOptional` documentation plus `@Type(() => Number)` query-string coercion. These responsibilities belong to the infrastructure (primary adapter/presentation) layer, not the declared application layer.

rationale: The file is assigned to the application layer only because of the **/dto/** and *.dto.ts patterns. It actually sits under primary-adapters/, its header comment says presentation/dto, and its only importer is inventory.controller.ts (infrastructure). Its work is all HTTP transport: @ApiPropertyOptional adds Swagger/OpenAPI docs, @Type(() => Number) converts query-string values to numbers, and class-validator decorators check the incoming request. These jobs belong to the transport/presentation adapter, which is infrastructure kind in this model, not to an application-layer use-case input contract. No business rules are implemented, but the transport and framework concerns don't match the declared application role. Confidence is moderate: NestJS projects often treat these decorated DTOs as acceptable application input contracts.
violation_messages: In class LowStockQueryDto, the @ApiPropertyOptional Swagger metadata and the @Type(() => Number) query-string conversion on threshold/page/limit are HTTP transport/presentation work, which belongs to infrastructure. They don't fit the application layer the file is assigned to.

rationale: The file is in the infrastructure layer (secondary-adapters/orm) and contains only one thing: a TypeORM persistence schema, InventoryEntity. It sets the table name, indexes, column types, a version column for optimistic locking, and timestamp columns. That is a persistence mapping, which is the job of the infrastructure layer. The file has no business rules (for example, no logic for low-stock checks or reservations), no transport code and no application orchestration. Fields like lowStockThreshold are only declared as data columns, with no behaviour attached.

The layer model places this file in the application layer because it matches both **/dto/** and *.dto.ts. Its one class, GetUserNotificationsDto, only describes a query and checks its input: page and limit for pagination, plus an optional status filter. That matches the role of an application DTO. It does not read or write data, handle routes or requests itself, or contain domain logic. The decorators come from class-validator, class-transformer and @nestjs/swagger. They only declare type conversion, input limits and API documentation; they do not run any framework behaviour. The page and limit bounds (at least 1, at most 100) are checks on the request, not business rules. The Swagger decorators are documentation for the API's interface, which brings in a little presentation metadata. NestJS projects normally put this on DTOs, and the project's layer model deliberately puts DTOs in the application layer. So this is not a responsibility that belongs to a different layer kind.

The file is declared as domain because it matched **/core/**. Its contents are a use-case workflow, which is application-layer work. CreatePaymentIntentUseCase.execute picks a payment gateway, calls an external gateway to create a payment intent, builds a Payment entity, saves it through the repository, and maps errors into UseCaseError. A domain unit should hold business rules and invariants, not workflows that call outside systems and save data. The class also uses NestJS's @Injectable() decorator, which is framework wiring. The path (/application/usecases/) and the .usecase.ts suffix also fit the application layer, so the layer model's overlapping patterns may have mislabelled the file. Judged against its declared domain layer, the file fails.
violation_messages: CreatePaymentIntentUseCase.execute() does application work inside a file declared as domain: it calls the payment gateway (getGateway, createPaymentIntent), saves through the repository (paymentRepository.save), and maps errors to UseCaseError. The NestJS @Injectable() decorator adds framework wiring. These responsibilities belong to the application layer.

rationale: The file declares a single data-transfer class, RecordCodPaymentDto, with declarative input-shape validation and API documentation metadata. The layer model explicitly assigns **/dto/** and **/*.dto.ts to the application layer, so an input contract fits there. It contains no business rules, no persistence, and no orchestration logic. The validation decorators (@IsNumber, @IsString, @Min(0.01), @IsOptional) only constrain input shape. The Swagger decorators (@ApiProperty, @ApiPropertyOptional) are transport documentation metadata with no behavior, and the project's own layer model treats such DTOs as application artifacts. The path (primary-adapters/dto) and the header comment (presentation/dto) suggest a presentation-adapter DTO. Even so, nothing in the file carries a responsibility that clearly belongs to a different layer kind.

The file declares one DTO class, UpdateCategoryDto, as PartialType(CreateCategoryDto). That is an application-layer job: it defines the shape of data passed into an update use case. The file has no persistence, request handling, routing or business rules. The PartialType helper from @nestjs/swagger only builds the partial type and carries API-doc metadata. It adds no transport behaviour, so it is not a responsibility that belongs to another layer. Import or dependency direction is out of scope.

ProductsController is a thin HTTP adapter in the infrastructure layer, and everything it does is transport or framework work. It uses NestJS routing decorators (@Get, @Post, @Patch, @Delete, @Param, @Query and @Body). It parses inputs with ParseIntPipe. It sets HTTP status codes with @HttpCode. It documents the API with Swagger decorators. It declares access requirements with @RequirePermissions and @OptionalAuth. It passes the caller context through with @CallerCtx. Each handler hands its work to an injected use case. The only data handling is in update(), which merges the route id into the DTO ({ id, ...updateProductDto }). That is plain request-to-command mapping, not a business rule. The visibility rules for inactive products appear only in the Swagger descriptions. The actual logic is left to ListProductsUseCase and GetProductUseCase, which receive the caller. The file has no persistence code, no domain invariants and no business decisions, so its responsibilities match the infrastructure (adapter) layer.

The file only declares an abstract port, `ApplicationLifecyclePort`, with one abstract getter, `isShuttingDown`. It has no implementation, no framework decorators and no persistence, transport or I/O logic. The doc comment says the concrete Nest-based version, ShutdownService, lives in infrastructure, which follows the usual ports-and-adapters split. You could argue that process lifecycle is an application concern rather than a domain one, so the port might sit better in an application or shared-kernel ports folder. Still, the file holds no misplaced logic of the kind the rubric names (persistence, transport, framework logic or business rules in the wrong layer). It is a pure abstraction with no dependencies, which fits a shared-kernel domain interfaces folder.

The file declares one TypeScript interface, CurrentUserPayload, with four fields: userId, email, role and an optional mustChangePassword. It has no behaviour at all: no persistence, no HTTP or transport handling, no framework decorators or calls, and no business logic that would belong in another layer. The interface describes who the acting user is, and a shared-kernel domain module can reasonably hold that. The name "Payload" and the files that import it (an identity decorator in primary-adapters and src/types/express.ts) hint that it began as an authentication token payload. Even so, the file itself is framework-agnostic and depends on nothing from transport or infrastructure. No ADR text was provided to say otherwise. I found no responsibility here that belongs to a different layer kind.

This unit is the standard NestJS root module. Its two files share one concern: putting the application together and serving a root health/hello endpoint. In src/app.module.ts, ApplicationModule pulls in the feature modules (ArticleModule, UserModule, ProfileModule, TagModule), sets up TypeOrmModule.forRoot() and registers AppController. In src/app.controller.ts, AppController has a single root() handler that returns a constant string.
