src/repositories/cardRepository.ts is in the persistence layer (infrastructure). All its functions do data access only. find, findById, findByTypeAndEmployeeId, findByCardDetails, insert, update and remove each run a parameterised SQL query through connection.query and return the rows or the result. None of them contains business rules such as expiration checks, blocking rules, password validation or balance checks. None handles HTTP requests or responses. The Card interface, TransactionTypes and the CardInsertData/CardUpdateData types describe how a card row is stored, which is normal for a repository. Setting password and originalCardId to null by default inside insert just maps optional fields to SQL NULL. Importing InsertDatabaseResponse from the services layer is an import-direction issue, which is out of scope here.

The file is in the persistence layer, which is an infrastructure layer. It does only data access. It runs a parameterized SQL query to find a company by API key and returns the first row. The Company interface is a row-shape type that goes with that query. The file has no business rules, no checks on whether a key is valid, and no HTTP or transport code. Those checks are left to the caller, the presentation-layer middleware. All of the file's responsibilities fit the persistence layer.

This file is in the persistence layer, which is an infrastructure layer. It only does persistence work. It declares an Employee row-shape interface and one data-access function, findById, which runs a parameterized SQL SELECT and returns the first row. It contains no business rules, validation, transport or HTTP handling, and no presentation logic. Declaring the row type next to the query is a normal part of a repository's data-mapping job.

The file src/repositories/index.ts is empty. It has no statements, functions or methods, so it cannot hold any responsibility that belongs to another layer kind. Nothing in it conflicts with its role in the persistence (infrastructure) layer.

This file only does persistence work, which is the infrastructure role. It defines row shapes (Payment, PaymentWithBusinessName, PaymentInsertData) and runs parameterized SQL through the database connection: a SELECT with a JOIN in findByCardId and an INSERT in insert. It contains no business rules such as validation, balance checks or amount limits, and no transport or presentation logic. Defining the row and insert types in the repository is normal for a data-access module. One thing to note that doesn't affect this rule: insert() doesn't await or return connection.query, so it doesn't wait for the insert to finish and its errors aren't passed back to the caller. That is a correctness bug, not a responsibility that belongs to another layer.

The file only does data access, which is what the persistence (infrastructure) layer is for. It defines a row type (Recharge), an insert DTO type (RechargeInsertData), and two SQL functions: findByCardId runs a parameterized SELECT and insert runs a parameterized INSERT. It has no business rules (no amount validation or card-state checks), no transport or HTTP handling, and no presentation logic. One note: insert() doesn't await or return the query promise. That is a correctness bug, not a responsibility that belongs to another layer, so it doesn't break this rule.

src/routes/cardsRouter.ts sits in the presentation layer. All it does is define Express routes: it maps HTTP paths and methods to controller handlers and attaches middlewares for API-key checks and request-body schema validation. Routing and request validation are presentation and transport work. The file has no business rules and no persistence logic.

src/routes/router.ts is in the presentation layer. It only creates an Express Router and mounts two sub-routers (cardsRouter and statementsRouter). Combining routes is a transport and presentation job. The file contains no business rules and no persistence logic, so its responsibilities fit its declared layer.

This file is a plain Express router in the presentation layer, and every responsibility it has belongs there. It creates a Router, maps HTTP verbs and paths to controller handlers, and chains the transport-level middleware for API-key checks and request-body validation. It contains no business rules, no persistence or data-access logic, and no domain calculations. Choosing which schema validates each route is input validation at the transport level, which is a normal presentation concern. No ADR text was provided to check against.

src/services/cardServices.ts is in the business (domain) layer, and its responsibilities fit that role. Every method (createCard, createVirtualCard, activateCard, getCardStatement, blockCard, unblockCard) applies business rules: employee/card existence checks, one card type per employee, virtual-card eligibility, activation only when no password is set, block/unblock state checks, expiration and password validation, and balance computation. Data access is delegated to repository functions. The file contains no SQL, no DB connection handling, no HTTP request/response objects and no framework code. There are two minor leaks, but neither amounts to a misplaced responsibility: 1. It reads the raw driver result with `insertResponse.rows[0]` and declares the `InsertDatabaseResponse` interface. This exposes the persistence result shape, but the file only consumes the data and does no persistence work itself. 2. It uses HTTP-flavoured error names ('badRequest', 'notFound'). These are only error classifications; no transport handling happens here. These are coupling smells, not responsibilities that belong to another layer, so the file passes.

The file passes. src/services/paymentServices.ts is in the business (domain) layer, and everything it does is domain or application work: - It runs the payment use cases (insertPayment and insertOnlinePayment). - It enforces the business rules: the card and business must exist, the card must not be blocked, and the password or security code, expiration date, business type and available balance are all checked. - It builds a PaymentInsertData object. - It saves the payment through repository functions (cardRepository.findById, paymentRepository.insert). The file has no SQL, database client code, HTTP request or response handling, routing or framework code. Persistence stays in the repositories, which are only called from here. Two minor points don't change the result: - The thrown error objects use names like "notFound" and "badRequest", which sound like HTTP terms. They are still plain domain error categories, not transport handling. - The file takes its input types (BuyOnPOSBody, BuyOnlineBody) from the controller. That is an import-direction question, which is out of scope for this rule.

src/services/rechargeService.ts (business layer, domain kind) has one method, rechargeService.recharge, which runs a recharge use case: it checks the card exists, rejects blocked cards, hands the expiry check to cardUtils.checkCardExpiration, and saves the recharge through the repository modules. Saving data is left to the persistence layer. The file has no SQL, database client calls, HTTP request/response handling or framework code. The thrown error objects use names like 'notFound' and 'badRequest', but these are plain error categories, not transport logic: the file sets no status codes and touches no response objects. Importing the RechargeInsertData type from a repository file is a dependency-direction question, which is out of scope here.

The unit is one file, src/app.module.ts. It declares only AppModule, the root module that brings together configuration (ConfigModule.forRoot), the database connection (TypeOrmModule.forRoot) and the DeliveryModule feature module. That is one coherent concern for a root module, so the files don't split into unrelated concerns. Two smaller issues are worth noting. First, the TypeORM setup calls config() directly instead of reading values through ConfigService with forRootAsync, which skips the ConfigModule abstraction that was just registered. Second, the entity list [Order, Deliveryman] is kept at the root rather than loaded from DeliveryModule (for example with autoLoadEntities). Both are common NestJS patterns. Both paths use the same config loader, so no rule or invariant is defined twice, and neither issue clearly fails the rubric for this unit.

This unit is one file, src/delivery/delivery.module.ts. It is the NestJS composition root for the delivery feature. It registers the TypeORM entities Order and Deliveryman, the two controllers (DeliverymanController and OrdersController), and the services and repositories for the deliveryman and orders sub-areas. Deliverymen and orders belong to the same delivery concern, and AddOrderToDeliverymanService and UpdateDeliverymansOrdersService show that the two sub-areas are tied together. The file holds no business rules or invariants, so nothing is duplicated. It also bypasses no module abstraction: it only wires providers, which is what a module file is for. The only inconsistency is cosmetic. The Deliveryman import uses an absolute path ('src/delivery/__models__/deliveryman.model') while Order uses a relative one ('./__models__/orders.model'). Two service files also lack the .service.ts suffix. None of this breaks cohesion or the module boundary.

Both files cover one concern: the delivery domain's linked entities. `Deliveryman` (deliveryman.model.ts) has a `@OneToMany` link to `Order`, and `Order` (orders.model.ts) has the matching `@ManyToOne`/`@JoinColumn` link back. Both are built the same way: a TypeORM entity with a static `create` factory and methods that guard its rules. Each class keeps its own rules: - The order name check lives only in `Order.checkName`, which `Order.create` calls. - The order limit lives only in `Deliveryman.addOrder`. - The rule against deactivating a deliveryman who still has orders lives only in `Deliveryman.changeStatus`. When `Deliveryman` changes an order, it goes through `Order`'s own method: `addNewMessageToOrders` calls `order.addInfoToDescription` instead of editing `order.description` directly. No rule is written twice. The two `changeStatus` methods share a name but apply different rules to different entities, so they are not duplicates. This module passes. All five files do one job: they are class-validator request DTOs for the deliveryman feature. Each DTO is used by deliveryman.controller.ts and by the one service that matches it. Six of the seven files cover one concern: deliveryman use cases. Each injects DeliverymanRepository, loads the aggregate with findDeliverymanByIdWithOrders, calls a method on the Deliveryman model and saves. update-order.service.ts breaks this. UpdateOrderService is an Orders use case. It injects OrdersRepository from src/delivery/orders/dal, takes UpdateOrderDto from src/delivery/orders/dtos and returns Order, so it belongs in the orders module and splits this module's boundary. Second, update-deliverymans-info.service.ts assigns deliverymanWithOrders.firstName and lastName directly. CreateDeliverymanService and UpdateOrderService have no try/catch at all. The same error-handling rule is therefore copied into several files instead of living in one place, and some files don't apply it.
violation_messages: UpdateOrderService is an Orders use case: it injects OrdersRepository from src/delivery/orders/dal, uses UpdateOrderDto from src/delivery/orders/dtos and returns Order. It belongs in the orders module, not in the deliveryman services module. | updateDeliverymansInfo sets firstName and lastName directly on the Deliveryman aggregate. The other services in this module change it only through model methods (addOrder, changeStatus, addNewMessageToOrders). Its `!== undefined ??` guard also means the assignment never runs. | Error handling is inconsistent with the rest of the module. createDeliveryMan has no try/catch, while sibling services copy the same catch block that returns error.message. rationale: The unit has a single file, src/delivery/orders/orders.controller.ts, and it covers one concern: HTTP routing for orders. OrdersController sends work to its injected application services (FindAllOrdersService.findAll, UpdateOrderService.updateOrder). It uses the module's own DTO (UpdateOrderDto) and the shared Order model the same way in both handlers. It has no business logic, so no rule or invariant is duplicated. It also doesn't skip its services by reaching into persistence or other lower-level code. One minor point, which doesn't break the rule: the update endpoint uses POST rather than PATCH/PUT. Import direction is out of scope.

The unit has one file, src/delivery/orders/dal/orders.repository.ts. It deals only with persisting the Order entity. The OrdersRepository class wraps TypeORM's Repository<Order> and exposes three methods: findAllOrders, findOrderByIdWithDeliveryman and save. Nothing in the file is unrelated to that job, no rule is copied, and the file does not go around its own abstraction. All four incoming services reach Order persistence through this class. That is consistent with the module boundary. I could not check whether any service also injects Repository<Order> directly, because those services are not unit files. Even if one did, it would not be a violation in this unit.

This unit is a single file, src/delivery/orders/dtos/update-order.dto.ts, and it has one concern: the validation shape of the request body for updating an order. Nothing in it is split into unrelated concerns. No rule is copied from somewhere else, and nothing bypasses the module's own abstractions. All validation goes through class-validator decorators. There is one small issue that does not break this rule: `description` has the @IsOptional() decorator but is typed as required (`description: string;`), while `isActive?: boolean` is typed as optional. That is a typing mismatch within the file, not a cohesion or duplication problem. The deliveryman service also imports this DTO. That is an import-direction question, which is out of scope here.

All three files handle one concern: application-level operations on the Order aggregate. Each is a single-purpose @Injectable service. Each injects OrdersRepository through its constructor and returns the Order model, so they use the same abstractions in the same way. No service skips the repository, and no rule or invariant appears in more than one place. UpdateOrderService hands state changes to the domain model (order.changeStatus, order.addInfoToDescription) and doesn't copy that logic itself. Two lookups use the same repository method, findOrderByIdWithDeliveryman. That is shared reuse, not a duplicated rule. This rule doesn't cover correctness, but two bugs in update-order.service.ts are worth knowing about. First, `updateOrderDto.isActive !== undefined ?? ...` uses `??` where `&&` was meant. A `!==` comparison always gives a boolean, never null or undefined, so the right-hand side never runs and the update never happens. Second, the code doesn't handle a null order coming back from findOrderByIdWithDeliveryman.

src/app.module.ts is a NestJS root module. It falls in the presentation layer through the **/*.module.ts pattern. Its only job is to wire modules together: it imports ConfigModule, TypeOrmModule and DeliveryModule and declares AppModule with no methods. It holds no business rules and no request handling. It has no queries, repositories or other persistence logic, only module registration. TypeOrmModule.forRoot does pass connection settings (host, port, credentials, synchronize, logging) and an entity list. You could argue those settings belong in an infrastructure config provider. Still, a NestJS module file is meant to register framework modules, and these values come from config() rather than being hardcoded. No ADR prose was given that would forbid this. The file therefore does not carry another layer's responsibility as the rubric defines it. That inline database setup is the only borderline point, so confidence is moderate.

The file sits in the domain layer and does contain real domain behaviour: the Deliveryman.create factory, the order-limit invariant in addOrder, the status rule in changeStatus, and addNewMessageToOrders. But it also carries persistence mapping, which is infrastructure work. @Entity('deliverymans') sets the database table name. @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') and @Column({ default: false }) set how keys are generated and what the column defaults are. The @OneToMany(..., { cascade: ['insert', 'update'] }) decorator tells the ORM how to cascade writes. The rubric explicitly lists persistence logic in a domain file as a failure. This is not about which way the imports point. The class itself defines how it is stored, so it mixes persistence work into a domain model.
violation_messages: The domain class Deliveryman holds persistence mapping, which belongs in the infrastructure layer: @Entity('deliverymans') sets the table name, @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') and @Column({ default: false }) set key generation and column defaults, and @OneToMany with cascade ['insert','update'] sets ORM write cascading. Moving this mapping into an infrastructure persistence model or schema would leave the domain entity free of persistence concerns.

rationale: The file sits in the domain layer. Its behaviour is genuine domain logic: Order.create, checkName (the name-length invariant), changeStatus, deliver, return and addInfoToDescription. But the same class also defines how orders are stored in the database, using TypeORM decorators. @Entity('orders') sets the table name. @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid') sets how the database generates ids. @Column({ default: true }) sets a column default. @ManyToOne with @JoinColumn({ name: 'deliverymanId', referencedColumnName: 'id' }) defines the foreign-key mapping, and the deliverymanId field exists only to hold that foreign key. These are persistence (infrastructure) responsibilities: table names, how keys are generated, column defaults and join columns. The rubric names persistence in a domain file as a failure, so the unit fails. The fix is to move the ORM mapping into a separate infrastructure entity or schema, or into the orders/dal layer, and keep Order as a plain domain class.
violation_messages: Domain class Order defines how it is stored in the database using TypeORM decorators: @Entity('orders'), @PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid'), @Column({ default: true }), and @ManyToOne/@JoinColumn on deliverymanId. Table, column, default and foreign-key mapping is a persistence (infrastructure) responsibility that does not belong in the domain layer.

rationale: src/delivery/delivery.module.ts is a NestJS @Module composition root. It declares controllers, registers providers and wires in TypeORM entity features with TypeOrmModule.forFeature. The layer model puts **/*.module.ts files in the presentation layer, and wiring and declaration like this is their expected job. The file has no business rules, no persistence queries, no transport handling and no domain logic. Registering TypeORM features is the standard way NestJS modules declare them, so it does not move persistence work into this file. Import direction is out of scope.

This file is a thin TypeORM repository that only does persistence work: it saves deliverymen, finds all of them, and finds one by id together with its orders. This file is a plain DTO in the application layer. It declares two string fields and puts class-validator rules on them that check input shape (IsString, IsNotEmpty). The file is a plain DTO in the application layer. It declares the input contract (optional firstName and lastName) and marks those fields with class-validator decorators for shape validation. The file holds a single application-layer DTO, UpdateDeliverymansOrdersDto. It has one optional string field, description, with class-validator decorators that check its shape. This file does the normal job of an application-layer use-case service. The service is a standard application-layer use case. This application-layer service has a single job: run the "find one order" use case by handing the lookup to an injected repository. The unit is a single file, correlation.service.ts, and it handles one concern: managing the correlation ID in the async request context. Both public methods, startNewCorrelationId and getCorrelationId, go through the same injected ContextStorage abstraction (via @InjectAsyncContextStorage) and the same shared CORRELATION_ID_KEY constant. Both unit files serve the single saga-registration concern. saga.module.ts wires the saga entities, RegistatorService and RegistatorController. registrator.controller.ts exposes three entry points (a RabbitMQ subscription, POST /saga and a cron timeout check), and each one goes only through the injected RegistatorService. The controller never touches the repositories or entities directly, so the module's abstraction is not bypassed. Neither file repeats a rule or invariant, and the queue and routing key both come from config. Two minor points do not amount to a split, duplication or bypass: CreateSagaDto is declared inline in the controller file, and the module is @Global() with an empty exports list, so the global flag has no effect.

Both files cover the same concern: read-side queries for the Report aggregate. They follow the same hexagonal pattern. Each class implements its in-port, receives its out-port through the constructor, and passes the call straight to it in execute(). Neither file duplicates a rule or invariant, and neither bypasses the module's port abstractions, for example by reaching into infrastructure. There are small inconsistencies: one query passes `params.id` and the other passes the whole params object, the parameter name `findReportByIdQuery` was copied into the second query, and the out-port method is oddly named `findReportWithPositionsByOutInPort`. One query returns ReportEntity and the other returns ReportReadModel, which is a reasonable split between entity reads and read-model reads. None of these breaks cohesion or the boundary.

The unit passes. Both files deal with one thing: storing and loading the Cart aggregate. CartMapper is the only place that converts between the domain entities (CartEntity, CartPositionEntity) and the ORM entities (CartOrmEntity, CartPositionOrmEntity). That includes the nested position mapping and setting positionOrm.cartId from the parent cart id. CartRepository implements the domain ports SaveCartOutPort and GetCartOutPort. It always goes through CartMapper.mapToORM and CartMapper.mapToDomain, so no mapping is done inline and the mapper is never bypassed. Turning outbox events into ORM rows is handed to the shared OutboxMapper rather than copied here. The transaction that saves the outbox rows and the cart together is persistence work, so it belongs in the repository. The domain's export() method is used for reading state, so the mapper never reaches into the entities' internals. No rule or invariant is duplicated. One small weakness: the outbox event parameter is typed as `any`. It doesn't change the module's coherence.

Both files are TypeORM persistence entities for one aggregate: the cart and its positions. They use the same abstraction, TypeORM decorators under the 'cart' schema, and each side of the relationship is declared once: ManyToOne/JoinColumn on the position, OneToMany with cascade on the cart. No rule or invariant is repeated, and no unrelated concern is mixed in. The two files import each other, but that is the standard TypeORM bidirectional-relation pattern, resolved lazily through arrow functions, so it does not break cohesion. A minor naming nit: the OneToMany callback parameter is called 'order' instead of 'position'. This affects readability only, not the rule.

Both interactors cover one concern, the cart use cases, and they follow the module's hexagonal pattern the same way. Each implements a port for calling in, takes outgoing ports as constructor dependencies, saves through the shared SaveCartOutPort, and leaves the state change to the CartEntity methods (createOrder, cancelOrder). No rule appears in both files and neither file bypasses the ports. Two smaller issues don't break the cohesion rule: CreateCartInteractor builds hardcoded test positions, and UpdateCartInteractor only cancels the order, so its name doesn't match what it does.

Both files are inbound use-case ports for the cart aggregate and serve one concern: they define the entry contracts that the cart controller depends on and the interactors implement. Both follow the same pattern, an abstract class with a single `execute` method that returns `Promise<CartEntity>`. Neither file repeats a rule or invariant, because neither contains any logic. Neither bypasses the module's abstractions: both use the domain `CartEntity` as the return type, and each has exactly one implementing interactor. One small stylistic difference: `CreateCartInPort` takes a bare `correlationId: string`, while `UpdateCartInPort` takes an `UpdateCartParams` object. That difference doesn't break cohesion or the boundary.

The unit has one file, src/delivery/board/offer/controllers/offer.controller.ts. Its job is to take incoming requests about offers and pass them to the domain. It has two entry points, a RabbitMQ subscriber (applyReportValidated) and an HTTP PATCH handler (updateOrderStatus). Both are thin: each maps its input to a command and calls an injected in-port (CreateOfferInPort or UpdateOfferInPort) without going around those ports or adding business rules. The PATCH handler builds its response with SavedOfferResponseDto.fromDomain, so it uses the module's response-mapping abstraction. The file contains no repeated invariant. There are two minor points. First, the method name updateOrderStatus does not match what it does, which is set the courier on an offer. Second, the event handler builds the offer name inline ('Report with ' + orderId) instead of using a mapper. Both are small naming and style issues that do not break the module's cohesion.

The three files share one concern: storing and loading the Offer aggregate. `offer.orm-entity.ts` defines the table schema. `offer.mapper.ts` holds the only code that converts between the domain object and the database row, in both directions. `offer.repository.ts` implements the three domain out-ports, and every read and write goes through `OfferMapper`. It never builds entities or rows itself, so the mapper is not bypassed. The field-by-field mapping, including the curierId/curierid rename, lives only in the mapper and is not duplicated anywhere. Writing the outbox inside the save transaction belongs to persisting the aggregate, and it is handed off to the shared `OutboxMapper` rather than reimplemented here. Two small points are not violations: the local variable is named `reportOrm` instead of something like `offerOrm`, and the two find methods don't handle the case where no row is found.

The module is meant to wire one hexagonal design: the controller calls in-ports, interactors implement them, and interactors depend on out-ports that `CurierRepository` implements. `curiers.module.ts` breaks this pattern for the "create courier" path. `CreateCurierInPort` is registered twice. The first registration uses a factory that builds `CreateCurierInteractor`, but it injects `CreateCurierInPort` itself rather than `CreateCurierOutPort`. The second registration maps `CreateCurierInPort` to `CurierRepository` with `useClass`. Because Nest uses the last registration for a token, the controller would get the repository directly and never reach the interactor, so the in-port/out-port boundary is skipped. Registering one token twice also means the wiring is not defined in one place. `CreateCurierOutPort` is registered but nothing injects it. That confirms the interactor was meant to depend on it and the module's own abstraction is not being used.
violation_messages: `CreateCurierInPort` is registered twice: once as a `CreateCurierInteractor` factory that injects `CreateCurierInPort` itself, and once as `useClass: CurierRepository`. The last registration wins, so the in-port resolves straight to the repository and skips the interactor and the in-port/out-port boundary. | `CreateCurierInteractor` should depend on `CreateCurierOutPort`, but its factory injects `CreateCurierInPort` instead. `CreateCurierOutPort` is registered and never used, which breaks the module's port abstraction.

rationale: All six files serve one concern: request and response DTOs for the curier controller. But they don't use the module's abstractions consistently. (1) The validation rule for the boolean field isActive is copied into two DTOs, and both copies use @IsString. UpdateOrderStatusDto validates its booleans with @IsBoolean, so the same rule lives in two places and both contradict the module's convention. (2) SavedCurierResponseDto.fromDomain fills a SavedCurierOrderResponseDto (orderDto), then returns orderReadonly (the domain entity's export) instead. This skips the module's own order response DTO and lets domain data reach the response. (3) The same method sets paymentDetails from commissionRate, so one source value feeds two response fields. (4) The request DTOs mark fields with @ApiProperty, but neither response class does, so API metadata is applied inconsistently.
violation_messages: ChangeCuriersStatusDto.isActive is typed boolean but validated with @IsString(). This duplicates the wrong isActive check in UpdateCuriersInfoDto and breaks the module's @IsBoolean convention. | UpdateCuriersInfoDto.isActive is typed boolean but validated with @IsString(). The isActive check is copied here instead of being defined once and correctly. | fromDomain builds a SavedCurierOrderResponseDto but returns orderReadonly (the domain export) instead, skipping the module's own response DTO. It also maps commissionRate into paymentDetails.

rationale: Both files cover one concern: persistence for the Curier aggregate. The mapper converts between ORM and domain shapes in both directions. The repository implements the domain's outbound ports and always goes through CurierMapper, so it never builds domain or ORM entities by hand and does not bypass the module's own abstraction. Order mapping happens only inside CurierMapper, nested under the curier aggregate, so that conversion rule exists in one place. There is minor overlap: createCurier and save have identical bodies (mapToOrm, then save, then mapToDomain). They implement two different ports, though, and neither one duplicates a business rule or invariant. The isActive filters differ by query (free couriers vs. active orders) and are not copies of the same rule. One possible bug is outside this rule's scope: findAllCuriers calls find() without loading the orders relation, while mapToDomain calls orders.map. Unless orders loads eagerly, that would fail at runtime.

Both files deal with one concern: read-side query use cases for the curier aggregate. They follow the same hexagonal pattern. Each class implements an inbound port, takes an outbound port through its constructor and passes execute() straight to that port. Neither file duplicates a rule or invariant, and neither skips the module's port abstractions, for example by calling persistence directly. There is one cosmetic problem that does not break the rule: in FindCurierWithCountOfOrdersQuery, the constructor field is named `findAllCuriersPort`, which looks copied from the other query. It actually holds a FindCurierWithCountOfOrdersOutPort. The misleading name hurts readability, but the module's structure is still consistent.

This unit is a single file, src/delivery/tracking/controllers/tracking.controller.ts, and it handles one concern: HTTP routing for tracking routes. Its two endpoints, createRoute (POST) and updateRoute (PATCH), only take the request DTOs and pass them to TrackingService. The file goes through the module's own service layer and does not touch persistence or business rules directly. It does not repeat any rule or invariant either. Validation stays with the DTOs, and the logic stays in the service.

Both files are request DTOs for the same route resource in delivery/tracking. Both use the same class-validator style, and both are used only by the tracking controller and service. That makes this one cohesive concern with consistent abstractions. UpdateRouteDto repeats the @IsString() rules for courierId and orderId from CreateRouteDto instead of deriving them (for example with PartialType). That overlap is small and normal for DTOs, so it doesn't count as a duplicated domain invariant. There is a drift to note: in UpdateRouteDto the optional fields (courierId?, orderId?) have no @IsOptional(), so validation still rejects them when they're missing. Deriving the update DTO from the create DTO would fix this. It's a validation-correctness issue, not a cohesion or boundary failure.

All four files are request/response DTOs for the warehouse controller. The three request DTOs (AddOrderDto, CreateWarehouseDto, UpdateOrderDto) all use @ApiProperty and class-validator decorators the same way. The response DTO (SavedWarehouseResponseDto with the nested SavedOrderResponseDto) maps from the domain through the entity's own export() method, so it doesn't bypass the domain abstraction. Both AddOrderDto and UpdateOrderDto validate isValid with @IsBoolean/@IsNotEmpty. That is a shared input check each endpoint needs, not a business invariant duplicated across files. No file splits into a second concern or holds business logic. Minor note: in the graph excerpt, warehouse.controller.ts doesn't import AddOrderDto, so it may be unused. That doesn't break cohesion.

Both files hold TypeORM persistence mappings for the same aggregate (a warehouse and its orders) in the 'warehouse' schema. They use the same abstraction, TypeORM decorators, in the same way. The two classes refer to each other in a bidirectional ManyToOne/OneToMany relationship. TypeORM needs that pairing for a bidirectional relation, so it is not a duplicated rule. The foreign-key join (warehouseId -> id) is defined only on OrderOrmEntity, and the cascade behaviour is defined only on WarehouseOrmEntity. Neither file mixes in an unrelated concern or works around the module's abstractions.

All four files are outbound port declarations for one concern: persisting and retrieving the WarehouseEntity aggregate. Each file declares a single abstract class with one abstract method. Every method takes or returns WarehouseEntity from '../../entities/warehouse.entity', so the files use the same abstraction throughout. No file duplicates a rule or invariant, and none contains logic that skips the module's abstractions. Two small points don't break cohesion. First, the 'Wh' abbreviation in GetLastWhOutPort doesn't match the other names. Second, GetWarehouseWithOrdersOutPort has no injector in the graph excerpt.

The unit has one file, tracking.controller.ts, and it covers one concern: the HTTP endpoints for the tracking feature. TrackingController is thin. Both of its handlers take a DTO from the request body and pass it straight to the injected TrackingService, which is the module's own service. Nothing gets around that service. The file doesn't touch persistence directly, contains no business logic, and doesn't repeat any rule or invariant that should live in the service or DTO layer. One small issue is naming. The handlers are called createRoute and updateRoute, and their parameters are createRouteDto and updateRouteDto, but the types they accept are CreateDeliveryDto and UpdateDeliveryDto, and the class is about "tracking". This is a naming mismatch, not a split in concerns or a broken abstraction, so the rule doesn't count it as a failure.

Both files cover one concern: input DTOs for the delivery resource. However, UpdateDeliveryDto declares orderId, truckId and targetPickUpPoint again with their own @IsString() validators. It does not derive them from CreateDeliveryDto (for example with PartialType), so each field's validation rule lives in two places. The copies have already drifted. In UpdateDeliveryDto those fields are optional in TypeScript but have no @IsOptional(), so class-validator still treats them as required strings. Unless validation is set to skip missing properties, a partial update will be rejected, which contradicts the optional typing. This duplicated invariant fails the rubric.
violation_messages: UpdateDeliveryDto declares the field validators (@IsString() on orderId, truckId, targetPickUpPoint) a second time instead of deriving them from CreateDeliveryDto (e.g. with PartialType). The copies have drifted: the fields are optional in TypeScript but have no @IsOptional(), so class-validator still requires them as strings and partial updates will fail unless validation skips missing properties.

rationale: The file sits in the presentation layer because it matches the **/*.module.ts pattern, so the layer model treats NestJS module files as composition and wiring. The only thing ContextModule does is declare a global NestJS module. It registers one provider (CONTEXT_STORAGE, set to a new AsyncLocalStorage instance) and exports it. That is framework wiring, which is what a module file is for. The file has no business rules, no persistence and no transport handling. The AsyncLocalStorage instance is created only as a value for the provider; the module contains no logic that reads or writes it. Even though the folder is named __infrastructure__, nothing in the file does work that belongs to another layer kind.

The file is a TypeORM persistence entity inside a dal/ folder, so it is declared as infrastructure. Its only job is to map the database schema: table name and schema, column types, primary key generation, and a one-to-many relation with cascade settings. All of that is persistence mapping, which is the role of the infrastructure layer. It has no business rules, validation logic, transport handling or presentation concerns. The isValid column is a plain stored field with no logic attached.

CreateVerificationDto is a plain data transfer object. It has four fields, each with a class-validator decorator that checks its shape. Defining input contracts with structural validation is the job of the application layer, and the layer model maps both **/dtos/** and **/*.dto.ts to that layer. The file holds no persistence, transport handling, framework wiring or business rules. One thing is wrong but outside this rule: `isFull` is typed as `boolean` but decorated with `@IsString()`. That is a validation bug, not a misplaced responsibility.

src/app.module.ts is the NestJS root module, placed in the presentation layer by the **/*.module.ts pattern. Its jobs are framework composition: it imports feature and infrastructure modules, sets up ConfigModule and TypeOrmModule.forRoot, and attaches ContextMiddleware to all routes in configure(). The TypeORM setup (Postgres connection, entity list, synchronize: true) is infrastructure configuration. Putting it in the root module is standard NestJS practice, and the file only declares settings; it contains no query, repository or persistence code. The file has no business rules, domain invariants or transport handling logic. A stricter reading could count the inline database connection settings as infrastructure work in a presentation file, but this is ordinary root-module wiring, so the file passes.

The layer model puts **/*.module.ts files in the presentation layer, so a NestJS module is meant to be the place where dependencies are wired together. CartModule only does that. It registers ORM entities with TypeOrmModule.forFeature, imports SagaModule, declares the controller and binds ports to their adapters. Its factories just build the interactors and pass in the injected ports. The file has no business rules, no persistence queries, no transport handling and no domain logic. Referring to TypeORM entities and repositories as DI tokens is still wiring, not doing persistence work. No ADR prose was provided to contradict this.

This file declares a single data transfer object, UpdateOrderDto, with one boolean field, isValid. The field uses a Swagger schema annotation (@ApiProperty) and class-validator checks for its shape (@IsBoolean, @IsNotEmpty). The layer model puts DTOs in the application layer, and carrying input data between layers with shape-level validation is a normal job for an application DTO. The file has no business rules, persistence, transport handling or framework control flow. The Swagger annotation is a small API-documentation concern, but in NestJS it is the usual way to declare a DTO, and the layer model itself classifies **/dtos/** and **/*.dto.ts as application. It is not a misplaced responsibility that rises to a violation.

This file is an outbound port (hexagonal style) declared in the domain layer. It has two parts. The first is `CreateSagaOutPort`, an abstract class with one abstract method, `createSaga`. The second is `CheckSagaApiDto`, a plain data shape with one field, `correlationId`. Defining outbound port contracts in the domain is a normal domain responsibility. The domain interactor `CreateCartInteractor` depends on the port, and the external `ExternalSagaApi` adapter implements it. The file has no HTTP calls, persistence, framework decorators or business rules that belong to another layer. The name 'ApiDto' hints at transport, but the type is only a framework-free contract shape with no transport behaviour, so this is a naming issue, not a misplaced responsibility.

This file sits in the domain layer, but almost everything it does is persistence mapping, which is an infrastructure job. The `Payment` class has no domain behaviour or business rules. It carries TypeORM decorators that set the database table name (`payments`), the database schema (`cart`), how the primary key is generated (`uuid`) and the column storage types (`bool`, `uuid`, `text`). That makes it an ORM table mapping rather than a domain model. That mapping belongs in the infrastructure layer, for example as a separate ORM entity or a repository-side mapping, with the domain `Payment` kept as a plain class. Whether domain may import `typeorm` at all is out of scope here. This verdict is only about the persistence work the file does.
violation_messages: Class `Payment` maps itself to the database through TypeORM decorators: `@Entity('payments', { schema: 'cart' })`, `@PrimaryGeneratedColumn('uuid')` and `@Column({ type: ... })`. This maps the class to the `payments` table and its columns, which is infrastructure (persistence) work sitting in a domain-layer file.

rationale: The file declares a hexagonal inbound port: a plain parameter interface (CreateOfferParams) and an abstract class (CreateOfferInPort) with a single abstract execute method that returns a domain entity. It has no persistence, transport, HTTP or framework logic. It has no decorators and no I/O, and it makes no business-rule decisions that belong to another layer. Declaring a use-case contract inside the domain/ports folder fits the domain layer's role in a ports-and-adapters design. The abstract class is used as a DI token by the controller and is implemented by a domain interactor. That is a binding detail and does not count as framework logic in this file. Import direction is out of scope.

The file only declares a data transfer object, `UpdateCuriersInfoDto`, whose fields are optional and carry declarative validation and API-documentation decorators. The layer model puts `**/dtos/**` and `*.dto.ts` files in the application layer, and a DTO that describes the shape of incoming data and its validation constraints fits that role. The file has no persistence, transport handling, framework orchestration or business rules. The Swagger `@ApiProperty` metadata is a common NestJS DTO convention and only annotates the data. It does not implement transport logic. One unrelated issue: `isActive` is typed as `boolean` but validated with `@IsString()`. That is a correctness bug, not a layer-responsibility violation.

This is a data-mapper in the DAL (infrastructure) layer. It only converts between ORM persistence entities (CurierOrmEntity, OrderOrmEntity) and domain entities (CurierEntity, OrderEntity). It copies fields one-to-one in both directions and does not compute, validate or branch on business rules. Mapping between persistence and domain models is a standard infrastructure job, so the file passes the rule.

This file is a TypeORM persistence mapping in the dal folder, which the layer model places in infrastructure. Everything in it is persistence work: the @Entity table and schema mapping, the @Column and @PrimaryGeneratedColumn declarations, and the @OneToMany relation with its cascade settings. It has no business rules, validation, domain behavior, transport handling or presentation logic. Cascade options on an ORM relation are persistence configuration, not domain rules. The file's responsibilities fit the infrastructure layer.

The file only declares an abstract outbound port, CreateCurierOutPort, with one abstract method, createCurier(curier: CurierEntity): Promise<CurierEntity>. It defines that contract in domain terms and has no persistence, transport, framework or business-rule implementation. Declaring an outbound port in the domain is the standard hexagonal/ports-and-adapters pattern. The persistence implementation lives in the infrastructure layer (CurierRepository in dal/ implements it). So the file's only job fits the domain layer.

The file only declares a NestJS module, DeliveryModule, that pulls together its submodules (CuriersModule, BoardModule and Tracking). Wiring modules together is framework composition, and the layer model puts *.module.ts files in the presentation layer, so this is the expected job for that layer. The file has no business rules, persistence or transport handling, and no other logic that belongs to a different layer.

The file is a plain DTO in the application layer (it matches **/dtos/** and **/*.dto.ts). It declares the input shape for a route update and uses class-validator decorators to check those fields. Describing and validating input is a normal job for an application-layer DTO. The file has no persistence, transport, framework wiring or business rules. The optional fields marked only with @IsString and not @IsOptional are a validation-correctness issue, not a responsibility in the wrong layer.

The file is a NestJS module declaration, which the layer model puts in the presentation layer (**/*.module.ts). Its only job is composition and wiring. It registers the TypeORM feature repository for Route, the TrackingController, and the TrackingService and ExternalTrackingApi providers. It holds no business rules, no persistence queries and no transport handling. Calling TypeOrmModule.forFeature is the framework's standard way to declare a dependency and is the usual job of a module file. It does not implement persistence. Every responsibility fits the role of a presentation/module file.

The file has one responsibility. It defines AddOrderDto, a data shape for input with three fields (name, orderId, isValid). Input checks on the fields come from class-validator decorators (IsString, IsNotEmpty, IsBoolean), and API documentation comes from @nestjs/swagger ApiProperty decorators. The layer model puts **/dtos/** and **/*.dto.ts files in the application layer, so declaring and validating a DTO fits that layer. The file has no persistence logic, no business rules or domain behaviour, and no request handling or routing. The ApiProperty metadata touches the API surface, but it is the standard NestJS way to describe a DTO and doesn't add a separate transport responsibility. The DTO sits under a controllers/ folder, but that location is an import or layer-placement question, which is out of scope for this rule.

The file sits in the infrastructure layer (dal/**). It is a TypeORM persistence entity: it declares the table schema, the column mappings and the ManyToOne relation to WarehouseOrmEntity. It has no business rules, no validation logic and no transport or presentation concerns. Even the 'isValid' field is just a stored column, not logic. Mapping data to the database is exactly what an infrastructure layer does.

WarehouseMapper sits in the DAL (infrastructure). Its only job is translating between domain entities (WarehouseEntity, OrderEntity) and persistence ORM entities (WarehouseOrmEntity, OrderOrmEntity). That is a standard persistence-adapter role, which belongs to infrastructure. The file has no business rules, validation, transport or presentation logic. For example, isValid is copied field-to-field and never computed. All of its responsibilities match the infrastructure layer.

This file is an inbound port in a hexagonal-style domain layer. It defines a plain parameter interface (CreateWarehouseParams) and an abstract use-case contract (CreateWarehouseInPort.execute) that returns a domain entity. It has no persistence, transport or framework logic, and no concrete behavior of any kind. Declaring port contracts inside the domain/core is a valid domain responsibility. A domain interactor implements the port and a controller consumes it, which fits the inward-facing port role.
